options.a: Retrofit isolation with utility-grade measurement of energy use at the ECM level
options.b: Retrofit isolation with key parameters measured and other parameters stipulated
options.c: Calibrated whole-building simulation checked against utility bills and submeter data
options.d: Whole-facility utility meter comparison adjusted for weather and static factors

distractorExplanations.b: Measuring key parameters while stipulating the rest is IPMVP Option A; Option B measures every parameter at the retrofit.
distractorExplanations.c: Calibrated whole-building simulation is IPMVP Option D, used when baseline or isolation data are not available.
distractorExplanations.d: Whole-facility utility meter analysis with routine and non-routine adjustments is IPMVP Option C, not Option B.

options.a: Audits the facility and sells the owner equipment, leaving performance risk with the owner
options.b: Provides the capital as a lender while the owner's own staff designs and installs measures
options.c: Locks in a fixed utility rate for the contract term in exchange for a share of the energy budget
options.d: Designs, installs, and often guarantees savings financed through future energy cost reductions

distractorExplanations.a: That is an equipment vendor or design-bid-build model; in an ESPC the ESCO takes on implementation and performance risk.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes third-party loan financing; the ESCO in an ESPC designs and installs the ECMs itself, often arranging financing.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed-rate supply deals are energy procurement contracts; ESPC payments come from verified energy savings, not rate locks.

options.a: Review design, witness testing, and verify systems operate per owner's project requirements
options.b: Write the basis of design and sequences of operation for the engineer of record to stamp
options.c: Approve contractor change orders and pay applications acting as the owner's construction manager
options.d: Replace TAB by measuring and setting design airflows and water flows at each terminal

distractorExplanations.b: The basis of design and sequences are written by the design team; the CxA reviews them against the OPR rather than authoring them.
distractorExplanations.c: Change orders and pay applications belong to the owner, architect, or construction manager, not to the commissioning authority.
distractorExplanations.d: Setting design flows is the TAB contractor's scope; the CxA reviews and spot-verifies the TAB report rather than replacing it.

options.a: Records the as-built sequences after turnover so operators can run the systems
options.b: Translates owner requirements into measurable performance criteria for systems
options.c: Lists the test procedures and pass/fail forms the contractor completes during FPT
options.d: Summarizes deficiencies found during construction and the dates they were closed

distractorExplanations.a: As-built sequences for operators belong in the systems manual and O&M documents produced at turnover, not the design intent.
distractorExplanations.c: Step-by-step procedures and pass/fail forms are functional test scripts, which are written to verify against the design intent.
distractorExplanations.d: A running list of deficiencies and closure dates is the commissioning issues log, a separate tracking document.

options.a: Equipment was set in place, wired, and started per the manufacturer's checklist
options.b: Air and water systems deliver design flows measured at each terminal and coil
options.c: Installed equipment matches approved submittals and nameplate data recorded at delivery
options.d: Systems and assemblies operate according to sequences and setpoints under simulated conditions

distractorExplanations.a: Setting, wiring, and startup are covered by pre-functional (construction) checklists, which come before functional performance testing.
distractorExplanations.b: Measuring design flows at terminals and coils is testing, adjusting, and balancing (TAB), not functional performance testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Comparing installed equipment with submittals is installation verification; FPT tests sequences and setpoints in operation.

options.a: Repeating commissioning on a building that was commissioned at construction to restore its performance
options.b: Ongoing monitoring-based process using permanent meters and fault analytics after turnover
options.c: Quality process applied from design through construction and turnover of a new building
options.d: Systematic process to improve performance of existing buildings whose systems were not commissioned

distractorExplanations.a: Repeating Cx on a building that was commissioned before is recommissioning; RCx applies to buildings never commissioned.
distractorExplanations.b: Permanent metering with fault analytics describes ongoing or monitoring-based commissioning, not a retrocommissioning project.
distractorExplanations.c: Design-through-turnover verification of a new building is new construction commissioning, not retrocommissioning.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: RCx uses documentation review, testing, and control corrections in operating buildings. Buildings that were commissioned before and have drifted are handled by recommissioning instead.

options.a: Owner's goals for comfort, energy performance, and system operability
options.b: Design narrative of how each system will meet the owner's requirements
options.c: Scope, schedule, roles, test procedures, and acceptance criteria
options.d: Measured savings baseline, adjustments, and reporting period equations

distractorExplanations.a: Owner goals for comfort, energy, and operability are the Owner's Project Requirements (OPR), a separate input to the Cx plan.
distractorExplanations.b: A narrative of how systems meet owner requirements is the basis of design (BOD), prepared by the design team.
distractorExplanations.d: Baseline, adjustments, and savings equations make up an M&V plan under IPMVP, not a commissioning plan.

options.a: Savings shortfalls in the reporting period caused by underperforming ECMs
options.b: Utility rate increases between the baseline year and the reporting period
options.c: Changes in static factors (e.g., area, shift schedule) that affect energy use
options.d: Metering errors discovered in reporting-period data after the savings were already invoiced

distractorExplanations.a: Baseline adjustments must not absorb ECM underperformance; shortfalls caused by the ECMs are exactly what M&V is meant to reveal.
distractorExplanations.b: Rate changes affect the dollar value of savings, not the energy baseline; IPMVP adjusts for conditions that change energy use.
distractorExplanations.d: Correcting bad meter data is a data-quality fix in the reporting period, not an adjustment of the baseline for changed conditions.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: IPMVP requires documenting adjustments when conditions change so savings remain attributable to ECMs. These non-routine adjustments are made independent of ECM performance.

options.a: The utility commits to hold energy rates fixed for the contract term
options.b: The owner and ESCO split measured savings by an agreed percentage
options.c: The ESCO commits contractually to meet agreed savings targets
options.d: The lender commits to cover debt service if the owner's budget falls short

distractorExplanations.a: Utilities do not freeze rates for ESPC terms; the guarantee is an ESCO commitment on energy savings, not on tariffs.
distractorExplanations.b: Splitting measured savings by percentage is the shared savings structure, a different ESPC model from guaranteed savings.
distractorExplanations.d: Lenders finance the project but do not backstop savings; the ESCO, not the lender, guarantees the savings level.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: Guarantees tie payments and remedies to measured or stipulated savings per M&V plan. Contracts often specify remedies, such as ESCO payments, if verified savings fall short.

options.a: Is performed once during the warranty period to resolve contractor deficiencies
options.b: Begins at design phase and ends at turnover once acceptance testing is signed off
options.c: Uses continuous monitoring and periodic re-testing to maintain performance over time
options.d: Targets existing buildings that were not commissioned at construction, using a one-time study

distractorExplanations.a: A one-time check during the warranty period is warranty-phase or seasonal commissioning, not an ongoing process.
distractorExplanations.b: A process that runs from design to turnover is new construction commissioning; OCx continues after occupancy.
distractorExplanations.d: A one-time investigation of never-commissioned buildings describes retrocommissioning, which OCx is being contrasted with.

options.a: Control sequences respond correctly to every operating mode and alarm
options.b: Installed equipment matches approved submittals and design capacities
options.c: Envelope air barrier meets the specified leakage rate under test
options.d: Hydronic and air systems deliver design flows and pressures

distractorExplanations.a: Verifying sequences through every mode and alarm is functional performance testing, which follows TAB.
distractorExplanations.b: Matching equipment to submittals is submittal review and installation verification, not testing, adjusting, and balancing.
distractorExplanations.c: Air barrier leakage is checked by blower door or envelope testing, not by hydronic and air balancing.

options.a: Owner goals for performance, comfort, energy, and operability
options.b: Design team's narrative of how systems will meet the owner's goals
options.c: Contractor's sequences of operation submitted for engineer approval
options.d: Commissioning scope, schedule, and team roles for the project

distractorExplanations.b: The design team's narrative of how goals are met is the basis of design (BOD), which responds to the OPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Contractor sequence submittals implement the design; they do not define the owner's own requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Scope, schedule, and roles are the contents of the commissioning plan, not the Owner's Project Requirements.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: OPR captures what the owner needs; basis of design shows how the team meets OPR. The OPR is used to guide both design and commissioning.

options.a: The commissioning plan schedule and roles issued before construction began
options.b: Test results, issues resolved, training provided, and recommendations for O&M
options.c: Measured energy savings by ECM versus the adjusted baseline for the first performance year
options.d: Contractor bid tabulations and change-order pricing for each trade package

distractorExplanations.a: The Cx plan schedule and roles are an early planning document; the final report records what was verified and handed over.
distractorExplanations.c: Savings by ECM versus baseline belong in an M&V or savings verification report, not the final commissioning report.
distractorExplanations.d: Bid tabs and change-order pricing are procurement and contract records, not commissioning verification content.

options.a: Selecting the 12-month period of pre-retrofit data used to build the baseline
options.b: Choosing the independent variables, such as degree-days, for the regression
options.c: Specifying which meters and systems are included in savings calculations
options.d: Setting the reporting period during which post-retrofit savings are verified

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing 12 months of pre-retrofit data defines the baseline period, which is separate from where the measurement boundary is drawn.
distractorExplanations.b: Selecting degree-days and other drivers defines the regression model, not which meters and systems sit inside the boundary.
distractorExplanations.d: The post-retrofit verification window is the reporting period; the boundary defines what is metered, not when.

options.a: Weather and occupancy regressed against utility consumption as the predictor
options.b: Utility consumption regressed against weather and other independent variables
options.c: Monthly peak demand regressed against utility rates to normalize cost
options.d: Post-retrofit consumption regressed against pre-retrofit consumption by month

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps the variables: consumption is the dependent variable, while weather and occupancy are the independent predictors.
distractorExplanations.c: Utility rates do not drive energy use; whole-building M&V regresses consumption on weather and operating variables.
distractorExplanations.d: Regressing post on pre consumption ignores the drivers; the baseline model uses weather and other independent variables.

options.a: Savings measured at the ECM with isolation meters under IPMVP Option B
options.b: Savings computed from whole-facility utility bills with routine weather adjustments
options.c: Savings predicted by a calibrated simulation model under IPMVP Option D
options.d: Savings assigned by agreement without direct measurement of that specific ECM

distractorExplanations.a: Option B measures all parameters at the ECM with isolation meters; stipulated savings are agreed values that are not measured.
distractorExplanations.b: Whole-facility bills with routine weather adjustments describe IPMVP Option C, a measured approach rather than stipulation.
distractorExplanations.c: Option D calculates savings with a calibrated model; stipulation assigns values by agreement without measuring that ECM.

options.a: Once, on an existing building whose systems were not commissioned at construction
options.b: Periodically after initial commissioning to restore performance as systems change
options.c: During design and construction, before the building is first occupied
options.d: Continuously through permanent meters and automated fault detection

distractorExplanations.a: Commissioning an existing building that was never commissioned is retrocommissioning; recommissioning follows a prior Cx.
distractorExplanations.c: Verification during design and construction is new construction commissioning, which precedes any recommissioning.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuous metering with automated fault detection is ongoing or monitoring-based commissioning, not periodic recommissioning.

options.a: Let the CxA assume design liability for systems it reviews and tests
options.b: Allow the CxA to direct contractors' means and methods during installation
options.c: Ensure the CxA can approve pay applications without owner involvement
options.d: Provide objective verification separate from design and construction teams

distractorExplanations.a: Design liability stays with the engineer of record; independence is about objective verification, not taking over design risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Means and methods remain the contractor's responsibility; an independent CxA verifies results but does not direct construction.
distractorExplanations.c: Pay application approval is an owner and architect function; CxA independence does not grant payment authority.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: Independence reduces conflicts of interest in identifying issues affecting energy and operability. Owners or programs such as LEED may require this independence.

options.a: Structured so the obligation resembles a service payment tied to savings
options.b: Structured as a capital lease where the owner takes title at signing
options.c: Financed through general obligation bonds issued and repaid by the public owner
options.d: Funded by an upfront appropriation from the owner's capital budget

distractorExplanations.b: A capital (finance) lease with title transfer is recorded as a liability on the balance sheet, the opposite of the intended treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: General obligation bonds are public debt carried on the owner's books, so they are not off-balance-sheet financing.
distractorExplanations.d: An upfront capital appropriation is direct budget funding; ESPCs exist to avoid relying on capital budget appropriations.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: Accounting treatment depends on contract terms and applicable standards; ESPCs aim to avoid capital budget barriers. Actual treatment depends on the applicable accounting rules for the owner.

options.a: Application after installation is complete, since pre-approval would delay the project schedule
options.b: Pre- and post-verification, often aligned with IPMVP or program-specific M&V rules
options.c: A signed ESPC with an ESCO guarantee before the utility will pay
options.d: Approval from the state energy code official before equipment purchase

distractorExplanations.a: Most custom incentive programs require pre-approval and a pre-installation inspection; applying after installation often forfeits the incentive.
distractorExplanations.c: Utility incentives are available to owner-funded projects too; an ESPC with an ESCO guarantee is not a program prerequisite.
distractorExplanations.d: Code officials enforce minimum codes; incentive eligibility is set by the utility program and its M&V rules, not by code approval.

options.a: Comparisons reflect ECM impacts rather than year-to-year weather differences
options.b: Savings are reported in dollars at current utility rates instead of in energy units
options.c: Baseline consumption is reset each year to the most recent 12 months
options.d: Static factors such as floor area changes are removed from the baseline

distractorExplanations.b: Converting savings to dollars is a pricing step; weather normalization adjusts energy quantities for weather differences.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolling the baseline forward would absorb the ECM savings; normalization keeps the baseline and adjusts it for weather.
distractorExplanations.d: Floor area and similar static factors are handled by non-routine adjustments, not by weather normalization.

options.a: A single lighting retrofit is isolated and its operating hours are measured on site
options.b: No baseline meter data exist and a calibrated simulation is required
options.c: Whole-facility or whole-system utility data are used with routine adjustments
options.d: Expected savings are small relative to the facility's total consumption

distractorExplanations.a: Isolating one retrofit and measuring its key parameter is IPMVP Option A, not a whole-facility Option C approach.
distractorExplanations.b: Missing baseline data that require calibrated simulation point to IPMVP Option D rather than Option C.
distractorExplanations.d: Option C needs savings large relative to facility use (often above about 10%) or they get lost in meter noise.

options.a: Performed at installation, after which electronic meters hold accuracy
options.b: Matched to the utility's billing cycle so readings align monthly
options.c: Defined in the M&V plan per manufacturer and program requirements
options.d: Deferred until savings fall short of the target in a reporting year

distractorExplanations.a: Electronic meters and CTs still drift; a one-time calibration at installation does not keep M&V data defensible.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing-cycle alignment concerns read dates, not calibration; intervals come from manufacturer and program requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for a shortfall makes calibration reactive; the M&V plan sets intervals in advance so data stay trustworthy.

options.a: The design-phase OPR and BOD drafts in place of the systems manual
options.b: Training, as-built sequences, trend access, and documented setpoints
options.c: Contractor punch lists and closeout invoices for the owner's accountant
options.d: Startup checklists, with sequences kept by the controls contractor

distractorExplanations.a: OPR and BOD drafts are design documents; operators need the systems manual, as-built sequences, and training.
distractorExplanations.c: Punch lists and invoices are construction closeout paperwork and do not help operators sustain commissioned performance.
distractorExplanations.d: Sequences must be turned over to the owner; leaving them with the controls contractor undermines O&M handoff.

options.a: The construction period while the ESCO installs and commissions the ECMs
options.b: The investment-grade audit period before the contract is signed
options.c: The first 12 months after acceptance, matching the installing contractor's warranty
options.d: Years after construction/implementation when savings are measured and guaranteed

distractorExplanations.a: Installation and commissioning make up the implementation period; the performance period starts after acceptance.
distractorExplanations.b: The investment-grade audit is the development phase before contract award, not the period when savings are guaranteed.
distractorExplanations.c: A one-year warranty is far shorter than typical ESPC performance periods, which often run 5 to 20 years.

options.a: Begins after occupancy by investigating systems that have drifted
options.b: Relies on utility bill regression to find deficiencies after turnover
options.c: Integrates verification throughout design and construction before turnover
options.d: Focuses on finding low-cost operational fixes in existing controls

distractorExplanations.a: Investigating drifted systems after occupancy describes recommissioning or RCx, not new construction Cx.
distractorExplanations.b: Bill regression is an M&V or benchmarking tool; new Cx finds deficiencies through reviews and testing before turnover.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-cost fixes to existing controls are the hallmark of retrocommissioning in operating buildings.

options.a: Baseline, reporting period, adjustments, measurement uncertainty, and savings computation
options.b: Contract financing terms, ESCO markup, and debt service coverage ratio
options.c: Equipment warranties, spare parts inventories, and preventive maintenance schedules
options.d: Design intent, functional test scripts, and commissioning issues log

distractorExplanations.b: Financing terms and markup belong in the ESPC contract and financial schedules, not the IPMVP M&V plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Warranties, spares, and PM schedules are O&M deliverables; IPMVP plans address how savings are determined.
distractorExplanations.d: Design intent, test scripts, and issues logs are commissioning documents rather than IPMVP M&V plan content.

options.a: The ESCO selects the best-performing fixtures to measure for the savings report
options.b: A fixed 5% of units is metered without regard to variability or precision targets
options.c: Units of different types and schedules are pooled into one sample to cut cost
options.d: Representative samples and statistical methods justify extrapolation to similar units

distractorExplanations.a: Hand-picking top performers biases the sample; IPMVP sampling must be random and representative of the population.
distractorExplanations.b: Sample size must be set from variability and precision targets (such as 90/10), not from a fixed percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixing unlike units and schedules violates sample homogeneity; each similar group needs its own sample.

options.a: The cost of energy the owner would have paid without the ECMs
options.b: The ESCO's installed project cost divided by the annual energy savings
options.c: The owner's actual utility bills paid during the reporting period
options.d: The baseline-year utility cost, without adjusting for current conditions

distractorExplanations.b: Project cost divided by annual savings is simple payback, an economic metric rather than avoided cost.
distractorExplanations.c: Actual reporting-period bills are what the owner did pay; avoided cost is what would have been paid without the ECMs.
distractorExplanations.d: Avoided cost uses the baseline adjusted to reporting-period conditions; the raw baseline-year cost skips those adjustments.

options.a: Estimated and documented so stakeholders understand confidence in reported savings
options.b: Excluded from the M&V report once meters have passed their factory calibration tests
options.c: Assumed to be zero when Option C utility bills are used as the data source
options.d: Limited to meter accuracy, leaving out modeling and sampling error

distractorExplanations.b: Factory calibration covers only instrument error; IPMVP still expects uncertainty to be quantified and reported.
distractorExplanations.c: Option C regression models carry statistical uncertainty even with revenue meters; it is not zero.
distractorExplanations.d: Total M&V uncertainty includes measurement, modeling, and sampling error, not instrument accuracy alone.

options.a: The most recent 3 months before installation, to reflect current operating practices
options.b: The lowest-consumption year on record, so the savings claim stays conservative
options.c: The period just after ECM installation, while operators are still adjusting
options.d: Representative operation, complete data, and absence of major anomalies or concurrent ECMs

distractorExplanations.a: Three months does not span a full operating cycle; baselines usually cover 12 months to capture seasonal variation.
distractorExplanations.b: Cherry-picking the lowest year is not representative; the baseline must reflect normal pre-retrofit operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-installation data belong to the reporting period; the baseline must describe conditions before the ECMs.

options.a: Require a capital budget appropriation before they can be implemented
options.b: Rely heavily on control changes, O&M practices, and persistence
options.c: Produce savings that persist without monitoring once they are set
options.d: Qualify for ESPC financing as long-lived equipment with 15-year lives

distractorExplanations.a: Operational ECMs are low-capital measures; a capital appropriation is typical of equipment replacement ECMs instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Control and O&M changes are prone to backsliding, so persistence depends on monitoring rather than lasting by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Long equipment lives describe capital ECMs; operational measures have shorter, persistence-dependent savings lives.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: Controls optimization and RCx measures are common operational ECMs with low capital cost. They depend on how systems are operated rather than on new equipment alone.

options.a: Project risk so the owner guarantees savings while the ESCO finances
options.b: Utility incentive payments between the ESCO's subcontractors by trade
options.c: Measured savings between owner and ESCO per agreed percentages after costs
options.d: Annual debt service between the owner's lender and the ESCO's lender

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the roles: the ESCO, not the owner, carries savings performance risk in ESPC structures.
distractorExplanations.b: Incentive payments usually go to the customer or ESCO under the program; shared savings split the measured savings.
distractorExplanations.d: Debt service is paid to lenders under the financing agreement; shared savings divide verified savings between owner and ESCO.

options.a: Replace the owner's approval of the M&V plan with a third-party signature
options.b: Verify reporting-period savings after the first performance year closes
options.c: Set the savings level the ESCO must commit to in the contract
options.d: Identify gaps in baseline, boundaries, and methods before implementation

distractorExplanations.a: Peer review informs the owner's decision; it does not substitute a third-party signature for owner approval.
distractorExplanations.b: Checking first-year savings is reporting-period verification; peer review of the plan happens before implementation.
distractorExplanations.c: The committed savings level is negotiated in the contract from the audit; peer review checks the M&V methods.

options.a: Test procedures, expected responses, and pass/fail criteria for each mode
options.b: Owner goals, comfort criteria, and energy targets for each system
options.c: Scope, schedule, team roles, and communication protocols for Cx
options.d: Deficiencies, responsible parties, resolution dates, and retest status

distractorExplanations.a: Procedures with expected responses and pass/fail criteria are functional test scripts, not the issues log.
distractorExplanations.b: Owner goals and energy targets belong in the Owner's Project Requirements document, not the issues log.
distractorExplanations.c: Scope, schedule, and roles make up the commissioning plan; the issues log tracks deficiencies to closure.

options.a: Air and water flows match design values at each terminal and coil
options.b: Installed equipment capacities match the approved submittal data
options.c: Control sequences and setpoints match intended operation over time
options.d: Meter readings agree with utility bills for the same billing period

distractorExplanations.a: Flow at terminals and coils is verified by TAB measurements, not by trending control sequences over time.
distractorExplanations.b: Capacity versus submittal data is checked during submittal review and installation verification, not by BAS trends.
distractorExplanations.d: Reconciling meters with bills is a metering QA step; trend verification checks sequences and setpoints.

options.a: The contractor's startup checklists, used in place of the sequences
options.b: Utility bill history, so the tests target the highest-cost months of the year first
options.c: Design intent, sequences of operation, and manufacturer requirements
options.d: The TAB report, so scripts repeat the measured airflow readings

distractorExplanations.a: Startup checklists confirm installation; test scripts must exercise the sequences of operation, not replace them.
distractorExplanations.b: Bill history helps target RCx opportunities but does not define test steps or pass/fail criteria for each mode.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeating TAB readings checks flows only; scripts test control modes and interlocks against design intent.

options.a: The contractor completes startup checklists and submits the final pay application
options.b: Substantial completion is certified by the architect, before functional testing is finished
options.c: The first utility bills after occupancy show consumption below the energy model's estimate
options.d: Systems meet OPR/design intent and outstanding issues are resolved or deferred with documentation

distractorExplanations.a: Startup checklists and pay applications are contractor milestones; acceptance requires verified performance against the OPR.
distractorExplanations.b: Substantial completion is a contract milestone and can precede Cx acceptance; testing must still be completed or documented.
distractorExplanations.c: Bills below the model estimate do not verify system operation; acceptance is based on testing against OPR and design intent.

options.a: Calibrated computer simulation models to predict baseline and reporting period consumption
options.b: Whole-facility utility meter data with regression adjustments for weather and occupancy
options.c: Continuous isolation metering of every parameter affecting the retrofit's energy use
options.d: Spot measurement of key parameters with other values stipulated by agreement

distractorExplanations.b: Whole-facility meter regression with weather and occupancy adjustments is IPMVP Option C, not Option D.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation metering of all retrofit parameters is IPMVP Option B; Option D relies on calibrated simulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Measuring key parameters and stipulating others is IPMVP Option A, the retrofit isolation key-parameter option.

options.a: Contractor warranty claims are filed before the first-year warranty expires
options.b: Energy improvements continue rather than degrading due to overrides or poor O&M
options.c: Baseline consumption is re-established each year from the most recent utility bills
options.d: Original design capacities are restored by replacing worn equipment

distractorExplanations.a: Warranty claims address equipment defects; persistence monitoring tracks whether operational savings hold up.
distractorExplanations.c: Resetting the baseline each year would hide degradation; persistence monitoring compares against a fixed baseline.
distractorExplanations.d: Replacing worn equipment is a capital project; persistence monitoring catches overrides and drift in RCx fixes.

options.a: Normal operation, alarms, seasonal changeover, and documentation locations
options.b: Construction means and methods used by each trade during installation
options.c: Design load calculations and equipment selection software procedures
options.d: Contractor bid pricing so staff can evaluate future change orders

distractorExplanations.b: Installation means and methods are the contractor's concern; operators need to know how to run the installed systems.
distractorExplanations.c: Load calculations and selection software are design-team tools, not operating knowledge for O&M staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Bid pricing is commercial information; Cx training covers operation, alarms, and changeover of the systems.

options.a: Measurement boundary, baseline period, and routine adjustment methods
options.b: Investment-grade audit scope and the list of ECMs to be evaluated
options.c: Annual savings reconciliation and the rate escalation used for dollars
options.d: Early contract end, performance shortfalls, and equipment ownership transfer

distractorExplanations.a: Boundary, baseline, and adjustments are M&V plan content; termination clauses cover early exit and asset transfer.
distractorExplanations.b: Audit scope and ECM lists belong to the project development agreement, not the contract termination provisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Savings reconciliation and escalation rates sit in the M&V and payment schedules, not the termination clause.

options.a: Savings from separate ECMs are added directly with no overlap analysis
options.b: Weather and occupancy changes shift consumption during the reporting period
options.c: Combined savings differ from the sum of individual measure savings
options.d: An ECM's savings decline over time as operators override its controls

distractorExplanations.a: Simply adding measure savings is the error interactive effects warn against, because one ECM changes another's savings.
distractorExplanations.b: Weather and occupancy shifts are handled by routine adjustments; interactive effects arise between the ECMs themselves.
distractorExplanations.d: Savings eroding through overrides is a persistence problem, not an interaction between measures.

cem-readiness-check-commissioning-espc-0.explanation: M&V plans must address interactions to avoid over-claiming savings. The difference comes from overlapping impacts, such as lighting retrofits changing HVAC loads.

options.a: Variables that change routinely, such as degree-days, entered in the baseline regression
options.b: Measured savings parameters stipulated by agreement, such as lamp wattage under Option A
options.c: Parameters held constant or adjusted such as floor area, production rate, or operating hours
options.d: Utility tariff components, such as demand ratchets and fuel adjustments, used to price savings

distractorExplanations.a: Routinely changing drivers like degree-days are independent variables handled by routine adjustments, not static factors.
distractorExplanations.b: Stipulated Option A parameters are agreed estimates for the ECM; static factors are site conditions outside the ECM.
distractorExplanations.d: Tariff components only price the savings; static factors are physical conditions that affect energy use.

options.a: Design review, commissioning plan, FPT, and O&M handoff for specified systems
options.b: Measurement and verification of savings for 10 years after occupancy
options.c: Envelope blower door testing at ACH50 for every new construction project
options.d: An independent CxA from a separate firm on projects of any size

distractorExplanations.b: Long-term savings M&V is not part of LEED fundamental commissioning; metering is addressed by separate credits.
distractorExplanations.c: Blower door testing is not a fundamental commissioning requirement; envelope Cx is part of enhanced or optional scope.
distractorExplanations.d: LEED lets a qualified owner employee or disinterested design-firm staff serve as CxA, so a separate firm is not mandatory.

options.a: A one-time walkthrough with portable data loggers installed for about two weeks
options.b: Monthly utility bill regression with no interval or BAS trend data
options.c: Design-phase energy modeling to set performance targets for turnover
options.d: Permanent or semi-permanent sensors and analytics to detect efficiency degradation

distractorExplanations.a: Short-term portable logging during a walkthrough is a classic RCx investigation, not continuous monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Monthly bill regression is too coarse for fault detection; MBCx relies on interval and BAS trend data.
distractorExplanations.c: Design-phase energy modeling sets targets before construction; MBCx monitors operating buildings.

options.a: Envelope air leakage paths at parapets and window perimeter seals from IR scans
options.b: Wiring code violations and arc-flash hazards in electrical switchgear
options.c: Undersized equipment selected during design load calculations
options.d: Stuck dampers, failed economizers, and short cycling equipment from trend rules

distractorExplanations.a: Leakage paths found by infrared scans are envelope diagnostics; FDD rules analyze BAS trends for HVAC faults.
distractorExplanations.b: Code violations and arc-flash hazards are found by electrical inspections and studies, not by trend-based FDD.
distractorExplanations.c: Undersizing is a design issue found in load reviews; FDD flags operating faults such as stuck dampers.

options.a: Cooling energy comparisons for hotter or cooler reporting periods versus baseline
options.b: Electric demand charges for peak months in the reporting period versus baseline
options.c: Domestic hot water use for changes in occupancy between baseline and reporting
options.d: Heating energy comparisons for colder or milder reporting periods versus baseline

distractorExplanations.a: Cooling energy is normalized with cooling degree days (CDD); heating degree days apply to heating energy.
distractorExplanations.b: Demand charges depend on peak kW and tariff terms; HDD normalization adjusts heating energy for weather.
distractorExplanations.c: Occupancy-driven hot water use is adjusted with occupancy variables, not with heating degree days.

options.a: Avoided energy, maintenance, comfort complaints, and equipment life impacts
options.b: Commissioning fees alone, compared against the total construction contract value
options.c: Energy savings alone, valued at the blended rate without demand impacts
options.d: First-cost premium of high-efficiency equipment selected by the designer

distractorExplanations.b: Comparing fees to contract value is a cost ratio; cost-benefit analysis must also count the benefits of Cx.
distractorExplanations.c: Counting energy alone omits maintenance, comfort, and equipment-life benefits that make up much of Cx value.
distractorExplanations.d: Efficiency equipment premiums are a design decision; Cx cost-benefit weighs commissioning cost against its benefits.

options.a: Baseline data are unavailable and a calibrated simulation must model the facility
options.b: Whole-facility utility data are adjusted for weather and static factor changes
options.c: Retrofit isolation measures every energy parameter continuously at the ECM with submeters
options.d: Retrofit isolation uses short-term or periodic measurement of key parameters and agreed factors

distractorExplanations.a: Missing baseline data with calibrated simulation is the IPMVP Option D situation, not Option A.
distractorExplanations.b: Whole-facility utility data with weather and static factor adjustments describe IPMVP Option C.
distractorExplanations.c: Continuous measurement of every parameter at the ECM is IPMVP Option B; Option A stipulates some factors.

options.a: Loses about 10 percentage points of efficiency compared with full load
options.b: Runs at its lowest efficiency point because losses peak below full load
options.c: Draws more input kW than at full load because slip increases at part load
options.d: Operates near its best efficiency point when properly sized for the load

distractorExplanations.a: Efficiency at 75% load is usually within about a point of full-load efficiency, not 10 points lower.
distractorExplanations.b: Efficiency falls off mainly below about 50% load; 75% load is near the peak of the efficiency curve.
distractorExplanations.c: Input kW drops as load drops; at 75% load the motor draws less power than at full load, not more.

options.a: Fan power drops roughly with the cube of speed when flow is reduced via speed control
options.b: Fan power drops in direct proportion to speed, so a 20% speed cut saves about 20%
options.c: Fan power drops with the square of speed, so pressure falls more than flow
options.d: VFD input current is in phase with voltage, cutting reactive power demand

distractorExplanations.b: Flow is proportional to speed, but power follows the cube: a 20% speed cut saves roughly 49% of fan power.
distractorExplanations.c: The square law applies to pressure; fan power varies with the cube of speed under the affinity laws.
distractorExplanations.d: A drive's displacement power factor is a minor side benefit; the main saving comes from the cube-law drop in fan power.

options.a: Reduce input wattage for the same delivered lumens
options.b: Increase input wattage but extend rated L70 lamp life
options.c: Increase efficacy, meaning more watts per lumen
options.d: Keep wattage the same while raising light output

distractorExplanations.b: Higher efficacy lowers wattage for the same lumens; L70 life is a separate rating unrelated to efficacy.
distractorExplanations.d: The question fixes light output, so the efficacy gain shows up as lower input watts, not more lumens at equal watts.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher lm/W means fewer watts per lumen, not more.

options.a: A constant-torque conveyor requiring full torque at low speed continuously
options.b: A pump with throttling valve control replaced by speed control
options.c: A cooling tower fan cycled on and off today to hold condenser water setpoint
options.d: A variable-torque HVAC fan with reduced speed at part load

distractorExplanations.c: Tower fans cycled on and off are good VFD candidates; speed control saves energy and reduces cycling wear.
distractorExplanations.b: Pump VFD retrofits replacing throttling valves are common ECMs.
distractorExplanations.d: Variable-torque fans are classic VFD applications with strong savings.

options.a: On resistive heating circuits, where current is largest during winter peaks
options.b: On LED lighting circuits whose drivers already operate near unity power factor
options.c: On the utility side of the meter, so the utility's transformer losses fall
options.d: At the point of reactive load causing low power factor, such as near large motors

distractorExplanations.a: Resistive heaters draw almost no reactive power, so capacitors there correct nothing despite the large current.
distractorExplanations.b: Loads already near unity power factor need no correction; capacitors belong near the inductive motor loads.
distractorExplanations.c: Utility-side capacitors do not reduce the customer's billed kVA or penalty; correction must be on the customer side.

options.a: Starting inrush current, which drops by roughly half versus standard motors
options.b: Stator and rotor copper losses, core losses, and stray load losses
options.c: Reactive power draw, raising power factor to near unity at every load
options.d: Mechanical drive losses in belts, couplings, and the driven load

distractorExplanations.a: Premium motors often have equal or higher inrush current; their gains come from lower running losses.
distractorExplanations.c: Premium efficiency targets real-power losses; power factor changes little and stays well below unity at light load.
distractorExplanations.d: Belt, coupling, and driven-load losses are outside the motor; NEMA Premium reduces losses inside the motor itself.

cem-readiness-check-electrical-lighting-.explanation: Premium efficiency motors use improved materials and design to lower electrical losses compared with EPAct or standard efficiency models. The comparison is against standard-efficiency motors.

options.a: Correlated color temperature
options.b: Luminous efficacy (lm/W)
options.c: Color Rendering Index (CRI)
options.d: Lumen maintenance (L70)

distractorExplanations.a: Correlated color temperature describes how warm or cool light looks, not how faithfully it renders colors.
distractorExplanations.b: Luminous efficacy measures lumens per watt of input power, an efficiency metric rather than color quality.
distractorExplanations.d: L70 lumen maintenance estimates hours until output falls to 70%; it says nothing about color rendering.

options.a: Limiting inrush current and mechanical stress
options.b: Reducing motor speed to match load as a VFD does
options.c: Correcting power factor at the motor terminals
options.d: Lowering voltage to cut running losses at full load

distractorExplanations.b: Soft starters ramp voltage only during starting; they do not vary running speed the way a VFD does.
distractorExplanations.c: Soft starters do not supply reactive power; power factor correction still needs capacitors or other equipment.
distractorExplanations.d: At full load the soft starter is bypassed or at full voltage, so it does not cut running losses there.

cem-readiness-check-electrical-lighting-.explanation: Soft starters reduce starting torque and inrush, lowering demand spikes and mechanical stress; continuous-run efficiency gains are typically small compared with VFDs. Energy savings at run conditions are usually modest.

options.a: Adding standard PF capacitors at the drive input to absorb the harmonics
options.b: Switching the utility meter to kWh-only billing so PF is not measured
options.c: Line reactors, harmonic filters, or true-RMS metering depending on severity
options.d: Lowering the VFD carrier frequency to eliminate line-side harmonics

distractorExplanations.a: Standard capacitors can resonate with VFD harmonics and fail; detuned filters or reactors are used instead.
distractorExplanations.b: The utility sets the tariff and metering; the customer cannot remove PF billing to avoid harmonic effects.
distractorExplanations.d: Carrier frequency affects motor-side switching noise; line-side harmonics come from the rectifier front end.

options.a: Photosensors detect sufficient daylight to meet target illuminance
options.b: Occupancy sensors detect no motion for the programmed time delay
options.c: The astronomical time clock reaches the scheduled sunrise offset for the zone
options.d: The utility issues a demand response signal during a peak event

distractorExplanations.b: Turning lights off after no motion is occupancy sensing; daylight harvesting responds to measured daylight.
distractorExplanations.c: Astronomical clocks switch on schedule, mostly for exterior lighting, without measuring actual daylight levels.
distractorExplanations.d: Dimming on a utility signal is demand response; daylight harvesting dims based on photosensor readings.

options.a: The application runs at high hours and benefits from higher efficiency
options.b: The motor runs a few hundred hours per year at near full load
options.c: The motor drives a constant-speed load with an across-the-line starter
options.d: The existing motor is lightly loaded but its utility rate is very low

distractorExplanations.b: A few hundred hours per year gives too little energy to pay back a premium motor, even at full load.
distractorExplanations.c: Synchronous reluctance and most PM motors require a drive; an across-the-line constant-speed setup does not suit them.
distractorExplanations.d: A very low utility rate shrinks the dollar value of efficiency gains, which weakens the payback.

cem-readiness-check-electrical-lighting-.explanation: Advanced motor technologies improve efficiency especially at partial load; high run hours improve payback on premium motor investments. These motors also hold efficiency well across the load curve.

options.a: Replace throttling with VFD speed control matched to system requirements
options.b: Keep throttling and add soft starters to cut inrush demand at startup
options.c: Install a larger, more efficient motor on the same throttled pump
options.d: Add PF capacitors at the motor to cut kVA while throttling continues

distractorExplanations.b: Soft starters only limit starting current; the throttling losses during operation remain unchanged.
distractorExplanations.c: A larger motor on an oversized throttled pump makes oversizing worse; the throttling loss itself stays.
distractorExplanations.d: Capacitors reduce kVA and PF penalties but leave kWh and real kW unchanged while the valve keeps throttling.

options.a: Reduced or eliminated PF penalty and lower I²R losses on distribution
options.b: Lower billed kW demand because real power falls with reactive current
options.c: Reduced kWh charges equal to the drop in kVA from 0.82 to 0.95 PF
options.d: Higher real power kW consumption for the same work output

distractorExplanations.b: Real kW stays essentially unchanged; PF correction lowers kVA and reactive current, not billed kW demand.
distractorExplanations.c: kWh tracks real energy, which barely changes; the kVA reduction does not translate into equal kWh savings.
distractorExplanations.d: Real kW for the same load should not increase; apparent kVA drops.

options.a: Certifying luminaires as meeting UL safety standards and electrical listing tests
options.b: Rating ENERGY STAR residential lamps for retail consumer labeling
options.c: Identifying tested LED products meeting efficacy and performance criteria
options.d: Setting lighting power density limits for commercial energy codes

distractorExplanations.a: Safety listing is done by UL and other NRTLs; DLC lists products that meet efficacy and performance criteria.
distractorExplanations.b: ENERGY STAR covers residential lamps and fixtures; DLC focuses on commercial LED products for utility rebates.
distractorExplanations.d: LPD limits are set by ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC, not by the DesignLights Consortium qualified product lists.

cem-readiness-check-electrical-lighting-.explanation: DLC qualification provides third-party verified performance data used in utility rebate programs and procurement specifications for commercial lighting. Utility rebate programs and specifications often require DLC-listed products.

options.a: Mechanical efficiency and reliability of power transfer to the fan
options.b: Motor nameplate efficiency, raising it to the NEMA Premium level
options.c: Fan curve shape, shifting the fan's best efficiency point to higher flow
options.d: Power factor at the motor terminals by reducing reactive current

distractorExplanations.b: Nameplate efficiency is fixed by motor design; belt maintenance improves transmission between motor and fan.
distractorExplanations.c: The fan curve is a property of the wheel and housing; belt fixes improve power transfer, not the curve shape.
distractorExplanations.d: Belt slip and misalignment are mechanical losses; they do not set the motor's reactive current or power factor.

options.a: Copper losses in the stator rise sharply as current falls at light load
options.b: Power factor improves at light load, increasing the reactive losses in the rotor bars
options.c: Fixed core and friction/windage losses become a larger fraction of input power
options.d: Stray load losses grow faster than output as the load fraction drops

distractorExplanations.a: Copper (I²R) losses fall as load current falls; it is the fixed losses that dominate at light load.
distractorExplanations.b: Power factor falls at light load rather than improving, and reactive current is not the main efficiency loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Stray load losses shrink with load; fixed core and friction/windage losses are what stay constant.

options.a: Time-of-use on-peak energy (kWh) charges
options.b: Power factor (kVAR) penalties
options.c: Fuel cost adjustment riders
options.d: Monthly billing demand (kW) charges

distractorExplanations.a: Short shedding events trim some on-peak kWh, but the charge set by the peak interval is the billing demand.
distractorExplanations.b: PF penalties depend on reactive power ratio; shedding non-critical loads mainly cuts the peak kW interval.
distractorExplanations.c: Fuel adjustment riders are priced per kWh and pass through fuel costs; they do not respond to peak kW.

options.a: How accurately the source renders colors versus a reference source
options.b: The visual warmth or coolness appearance of the light source
options.c: The operating temperature of the LED junction at rated current
options.d: The spectral power output used to compute luminous efficacy

distractorExplanations.a: Color fidelity compared with a reference source is the Color Rendering Index, not correlated color temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Junction temperature is a thermal rating that affects LED life; CCT in kelvin describes light color appearance.
distractorExplanations.d: Spectral output feeds efficacy calculations, but CCT only describes whether light appears warm or cool.

options.a: Maintained illuminance meets task requirements after wattage reduction
options.b: Fixture counts match the utility rebate application before installation
options.c: Lighting power density stays above the energy code minimum allowance
options.d: Color temperature of new fixtures matches the existing lamps exactly

distractorExplanations.b: Fixture counts matter for rebates, but a light-level audit is about maintained illuminance for tasks.
distractorExplanations.c: Energy codes set maximum LPD allowances, not minimums; illuminance targets come from IES task guidance.
distractorExplanations.d: Matching CCT is a design preference; the audit checks foot-candle levels so tasks stay properly lit.

options.a: Raising the efficacy of each luminaire so it produces more lumens per watt consumed
options.b: Adjusting output to required illuminance rather than maintaining uniform over-lighting
options.c: Switching fixtures off when occupancy sensors detect a vacant space
options.d: Dimming perimeter fixtures in response to measured daylight levels

distractorExplanations.a: Efficacy is a fixed product property; task tuning lowers set output levels without changing lumens per watt.
distractorExplanations.c: Switching off in vacant spaces is occupancy control; task tuning sets a lower maximum output while occupied.
distractorExplanations.d: Dimming on measured daylight is daylight harvesting; task tuning trims output to need regardless of daylight.

options.a: Rewinding with smaller wire gauge or increased slot fill losses versus factory design
options.b: Using manufacturer-specified varnish and wire for identical slot design
options.c: Testing insulation resistance and running a surge comparison test after rewind
options.d: Balancing the rotor and replacing worn bearings during the rewind

distractorExplanations.c: Insulation resistance and surge testing verify rewind quality; they do not reduce the motor's efficiency.
distractorExplanations.d: Rotor balancing and bearing replacement are good rewind practice that help preserve efficiency and reliability.
distractorExplanations.b: Proper rewinds to OEM specs maintain efficiency.

options.a: Elevator motors are DC machines that a standard AC drive cannot control
options.b: Elevators require specialized controls and safety codes not met by generic VFD retrofits
options.c: Elevator hoists are variable-torque loads whose VFD savings would be too small to matter
options.d: Regenerated energy from descending cars would be billed by the utility

distractorExplanations.a: Many modern elevators use AC motors, and code and safety integration, not motor type, is the real obstacle.
distractorExplanations.c: Hoists are constant-torque loads; elevator drives can save energy, but must be manufacturer-integrated for safety.
distractorExplanations.d: Regeneration reduces net energy use; the concern with generic VFDs is safety, controls, and code compliance.

options.a: Data center IT load supplied by a single UPS with no redundancy
options.b: Non-critical process loads or HVAC with thermal storage buffer
options.c: Hospital operating room HVAC that must hold pressure and humidity
options.d: Fire pump and emergency lighting loads tested during the event

distractorExplanations.a: Non-redundant IT load cannot be shed without risking an outage, so it is a poor curtailment candidate.
distractorExplanations.c: Operating room HVAC must hold pressure relationships and humidity for infection control during any event.
distractorExplanations.d: Life safety loads such as fire pumps and egress lighting must stay available and are excluded from curtailment.

options.a: Estimated hours until 70% of a sample of LED drivers have failed
options.b: Percentage of initial lumens remaining after 70,000 operating hours
options.c: Estimated hours until light output falls to 70% of initial lumens
options.d: Hours until the fixture's efficacy drops to 70 lumens per watt

distractorExplanations.a: Driver failure rates are a separate reliability metric; L70 tracks lumen depreciation of the light source.
distractorExplanations.b: L70 is the hours to reach 70% of initial lumens, not the lumen percentage left at a fixed 70,000 hours.
distractorExplanations.d: The 70 in L70 is a percentage of initial lumens, not an efficacy value in lumens per watt.

options.a: LED signs are switched off by occupancy sensors when spaces are empty
options.b: LED signs run on battery power, removing them from the electric bill
options.c: LED exit signs use far fewer watts for equivalent visibility 24/7
options.d: Incandescent signs have a higher power factor that raises kVA billing

distractorExplanations.a: Exit signs must stay illuminated continuously by code; occupancy control of exit signs is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.b: Batteries only provide backup during outages; normal operation draws utility power continuously.
distractorExplanations.d: Incandescent lamps are resistive with near-unity power factor; savings come from much lower wattage.

options.a: Long-term motor energy consumption across the installed base turnover
options.b: Peak demand charges in the first year, before any motors are replaced
options.c: Motor repair costs, since premium motors are not eligible for rewinding
options.d: Reactive power penalties, since premium motors run at unity power factor

distractorExplanations.b: A replacement policy acts as motors fail over years; it gives no first-year demand cut before replacements occur.
distractorExplanations.c: Premium motors can be rewound to proper standards; the policy targets energy losses, not repair eligibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Premium motors still run below unity power factor; the policy cuts real-power losses, not reactive penalties.

options.a: Demand meters record instantaneous peaks rather than averages
options.b: Nameplate ratings understate the actual running load of motors
options.c: Not all equipment runs simultaneously at nameplate load
options.d: Billed demand is measured in kVA while connected load is in kW

distractorExplanations.a: Demand is usually a 15- or 30-minute average, and instantaneous peaks would raise billed demand, not lower it.
distractorExplanations.b: Motors usually run below nameplate, so nameplate overstates load; understating would push demand above connected load.
distractorExplanations.d: kVA is equal to or larger than kW, so kVA billing would raise billed demand relative to connected kW.

options.a: Switch entire warehouse zones on a fixed time schedule set to shift start and end
options.b: Dim or switch fixtures in unoccupied aisles while maintaining safety minimums
options.c: Hold emergency egress fixtures at full output and switch off the rest
options.d: Raise fixture output when forklifts enter to offset lumen depreciation

distractorExplanations.a: Zone time schedules save only outside shifts; aisle controls respond to actual aisle occupancy during shifts.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving only egress fixtures on can drop vacant aisles below safety minimums; aisle controls dim to a set level.
distractorExplanations.d: Lumen depreciation is handled by tuning or maintenance factors; aisle controls dim vacant aisles to save energy.

options.a: kW draw at comparable airflow or static pressure setpoints
options.b: Motor full-load amps recorded once before and once after the VFD
options.c: VFD output frequency compared with the original 60 Hz motor speed
options.d: Annual facility kWh from utility bills with no weather adjustment

distractorExplanations.b: Single amp readings ignore voltage, power factor, and duty point; true kW at matched flow or pressure is needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency indicates speed, not power; savings must be shown as kW at comparable airflow or pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Unadjusted facility bills mix many loads and weather effects; one fan's savings cannot be isolated that way.

options.a: Billed demand peaks equal to locked-rotor kW for the whole month
options.b: Lower running efficiency for the motor once it reaches full speed
options.c: Short-duration demand spikes and voltage dip on weak feeders
options.d: Power factor penalties because inrush is mostly reactive current

distractorExplanations.a: Demand is averaged over 15 to 30 minutes, so a few seconds of inrush adds only a small spike, not locked-rotor kW.
distractorExplanations.b: Starting method does not change running efficiency once the motor is up to speed.
distractorExplanations.d: PF penalties are based on billing-period kVAR or kVA, so brief starting current has little effect on them.

options.a: Fixtures with the highest lumen output per fixture, independent of wattage
options.b: Efficient products delivering required lumens with lower connected wattage
options.c: Products with the lowest wattage per fixture, without checking lumen output
options.d: Fixtures meeting the specified CRI and CCT for occupant visual comfort

distractorExplanations.a: Maximizing lumens per fixture ignores input power; an efficacy spec ties output to the watts consumed.
distractorExplanations.c: Low wattage alone can mean under-lighting; efficacy requires delivering required lumens per watt.
distractorExplanations.d: CRI and CCT are color quality specs; efficacy (lm/W) is what ensures efficient light output per watt.

options.a: It lowers kWh charges by the same percentage as the kVA reduction
options.b: It reduces real kW demand, which kVA tariffs bill at a higher rate
options.c: Reducing reactive power lowers billed apparent demand directly
options.d: It lowers the demand ratchet percentage written into the tariff

distractorExplanations.a: kWh reflects real energy, which barely changes with PF correction; only the billed kVA demand drops.
distractorExplanations.b: PF correction leaves real kW almost unchanged; the saving comes from lower apparent kVA on the bill.
distractorExplanations.d: The ratchet percentage is fixed in the tariff; PF correction lowers the kVA value the ratchet applies to.

options.a: Group relamping on the fluorescent schedule of about every 3 to 4 years to cut labor cost
options.b: Run-to-failure with no inspections, since LED arrays rarely fail before L70
options.c: Preventive inspection and spot replacement based on failure or lumen depreciation monitoring
options.d: Group replacement of all drivers at the 50,000-hour L70 rating in one visit

distractorExplanations.a: Fluorescent group-relamp intervals reflect short lamp life; applying them to LEDs discards most of their useful life.
distractorExplanations.b: Drivers often fail before the arrays reach L70, so skipping inspection leaves outages and dim fixtures unnoticed.
distractorExplanations.d: L70 rates the light source, not driver life; blanket driver swaps at L70 ignore actual condition and failures.

options.a: Motor nameplate horsepower alone, matching the drive hp rating
options.b: Motor locked-rotor current, since the drive must supply full inrush
options.c: The feeder breaker rating serving the motor control center
options.d: Motor full-load current and manufacturer/heating requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Drive hp ratings assume typical motor current; sizing must use actual motor FLA, which can exceed the hp table value.
distractorExplanations.b: A VFD ramps the motor up and avoids locked-rotor inrush, so it is not sized to supply locked-rotor current.
distractorExplanations.c: The feeder breaker protects the MCC circuit; VFD current rating must match the motor full-load current.

cem-readiness-check-electrical-lighting-.explanation: VFD sizing follows motor FLA, service factor, and application duty; undersizing causes nuisance trips and overheating. Sizing should also include the drive's overload capability for the application.

options.a: Outdoor dry-bulb temperature is below the return air temperature, so outside air can replace return air
options.b: Outdoor wet-bulb temperature is low enough to produce chilled water without mechanical refrigeration
options.c: Outdoor dew point is low enough that the cooling coil runs dry with no latent load left to remove
options.d: Condenser water leaving the tower is above chilled water return, so the chiller can be bypassed

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing outdoor dry-bulb with return air is the airside economizer test; a waterside economizer depends on wet-bulb.
distractorExplanations.c: A dry coil reduces latent load but still needs chilled water; free cooling depends on the tower making cold enough water.
distractorExplanations.d: Tower water must be colder than chilled water return for free cooling; warmer water cannot cool the loop.

options.a: Raising supply air temperature at every load so reheat is not needed in any zone
options.b: Delivering constant airflow while varying supply air temperature at each zone
options.c: Increasing outdoor air at part load so the economizer handles more of the building's cooling load
options.d: Reducing supply fan energy and minimizing simultaneous cooling and reheat at partial loads

distractorExplanations.a: Supply air temperature reset is an add-on strategy; VAV savings come from reducing airflow, fan power, and reheat.
distractorExplanations.b: Constant airflow with varying temperature describes constant-volume systems, the baseline VAV improves on.
distractorExplanations.c: Economizer operation is separate from VAV; minimum outdoor air is set by ventilation needs, not part load.

options.a: Chilled water supply setpoint reset upward by 2°F during a mild-weather period
options.b: Entering condenser water about 5°F below design because the tower is oversized
options.c: Evaporator water flow at design with a clean, recently brushed evaporator
options.d: Elevated condenser water temperature or fouled condenser tubes raising lift

distractorExplanations.a: Raising chilled water supply temperature reduces lift and improves kW/ton, so it cannot explain worse efficiency.
distractorExplanations.b: Colder entering condenser water lowers lift and improves kW/ton; it would not push the chiller to 0.72 kW/ton.
distractorExplanations.c: Design evaporator flow and clean tubes support rated efficiency; they point away from the cause of high kW/ton.

options.a: The difference between entering and leaving condenser water temperature at the tower
options.b: The difference between leaving condenser water temperature and ambient dry-bulb temperature
options.c: The difference between leaving condenser water temperature and ambient wet-bulb temperature
options.d: The difference between supply and return chilled water temperature

distractorExplanations.a: Entering minus leaving condenser water temperature is the cooling tower range, not the approach.
distractorExplanations.b: Evaporative towers are limited by wet-bulb, not dry-bulb; approach is measured against ambient wet-bulb.
distractorExplanations.d: Supply/return delta-T describes chilled water loop performance, not tower approach.

options.a: Holding duct static at the design setpoint and trimming flow with box dampers
options.b: Resetting supply air temperature upward whenever zone dampers are mostly closed
options.c: Lowering duct static setpoint when zone dampers are sufficiently open
options.d: Raising static setpoint during low occupancy to keep VAV boxes controllable

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed design static setpoint is the baseline that reset improves on; throttling at the boxes wastes fan energy.
distractorExplanations.b: Raising supply air temperature is SAT reset, a different strategy that can increase fan airflow.
distractorExplanations.d: Low occupancy means lower airflow and allows a lower static setpoint, not a higher one.

options.a: Outdoor air temperature or building load to reduce piping and boiler losses
options.b: Indoor zone humidity so supply water stays above the space dew point
options.c: Boiler stack temperature to keep flue gas from condensing in the vent
options.d: Time of day only, using a fixed schedule for occupied and unoccupied periods

distractorExplanations.b: Keeping water above dew point is a radiant cooling or chilled water concern, not heating hot water reset.
distractorExplanations.c: Minimum return temperature protects non-condensing boilers, but reset itself follows outdoor air or load.
distractorExplanations.d: A time schedule gives occupied and setback setpoints; reset continuously varies supply temperature with load.

options.a: Chilled water flow too low for the load, starving coils at the loop end
options.b: Chiller evaporator fouling that raises the leaving chilled water supply temperature
options.c: Supply water setpoint too low, causing chiller surge at light load
options.d: Excessive flow relative to load, often from oversized pumps or poor valve control

distractorExplanations.a: Too little flow for the load produces a high delta-T, the opposite of low delta-T syndrome.
distractorExplanations.b: Evaporator fouling hurts chiller heat transfer but does not cause the excess flow behind low delta-T.
distractorExplanations.c: Surge is a compressor stability issue at low lift and load; low delta-T is a loop flow-to-load mismatch.

options.a: Flow is constant at design and the pump runs at full speed most hours
options.b: System head is mostly static lift, such as pumping up to an open tower at high elevation
options.c: The pump is already trimmed to the duty point with three-way coil valves
options.d: System head varies with flow and pumps operate at part load for extended periods

distractorExplanations.a: Constant design flow at full speed leaves no room for speed reduction, so the VFD saves little.
distractorExplanations.b: Static lift does not fall with flow, so speed can drop only slightly and cube-law savings are limited.
distractorExplanations.c: Three-way valves keep loop flow constant, so a VFD has little variable flow to follow without valve changes.

options.a: Using outdoor air for free cooling when outdoor enthalpy is below return
options.b: Raising ventilation when CO2 falls below setpoint to pre-flush the space
options.c: Modulating outdoor air intake based on measured or estimated occupancy
options.d: Recovering heat from exhaust air to precondition the ventilation air

distractorExplanations.a: Free cooling with outdoor air based on enthalpy is economizer control, not demand controlled ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: DCV reduces outdoor air when CO2 is low; raising it below setpoint reverses the control logic.
distractorExplanations.d: Exhaust heat recovery is an ERV or HRV function; DCV changes the amount of outdoor air brought in.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-00.explanation: DCV trims ventilation when actual occupancy is below design, lowering conditioning load while maintaining code-minimum air quality. This replaces ventilating continuously for fixed design occupancy.

options.a: Outdoor air is a small share of supply and the site sees mostly mild, temperate weather
options.b: Most exhaust air comes from kitchen hoods and fume hoods that cannot share a wheel with supply
options.c: The supply and exhaust air streams are located on opposite ends of the building
options.d: There is a significant temperature or enthalpy difference between exhaust and outdoor air streams

distractorExplanations.a: Low outdoor air fractions and mild weather leave little recoverable energy, which makes an ERV hard to justify.
distractorExplanations.b: Grease and fume exhaust risk contaminating supply air through a wheel, so ERVs are usually excluded there.
distractorExplanations.c: Separated airstreams require long ductwork or run-around loops, which raise cost and reduce ERV value.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-01.explanation: ERVs transfer sensible and/or latent energy between exhaust and supply streams, reducing heating and cooling loads when conditions differ. Adequate annual run hours are also needed for a good payback.

options.a: Have lower first cost and simpler maintenance but may have higher unit energy use at scale
options.b: Achieve lower kW/ton than a central water-cooled plant of the same capacity
options.c: Have higher first cost but lower energy use because each zone gets its own packaged unit
options.d: Need a dedicated chilled water loop and cooling tower to serve each unit

distractorExplanations.b: Air-cooled packaged units generally have higher kW/ton than water-cooled central plants of similar capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: RTUs usually cost less up front, not more, and many small units are not inherently more efficient.
distractorExplanations.d: Packaged rooftop units have self-contained DX refrigeration and need no chilled water loop or cooling tower.

options.a: Horizontally to the left (decreasing dry-bulb) at constant humidity ratio
options.b: Horizontally to the right (increasing dry-bulb) at constant humidity ratio
options.c: Vertically downward (decreasing humidity ratio) at constant dry-bulb
options.d: Down and to the left along the saturation curve as moisture condenses

distractorExplanations.b: Moving right at constant humidity ratio is sensible heating, which raises dry-bulb rather than lowering it.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving straight down at constant dry-bulb is pure dehumidification, which removes moisture without cooling.
distractorExplanations.d: Following the saturation curve occurs with condensation, which is cooling with dehumidification.

options.a: Suction pressure alone, compared against a standard refrigerant pressure-temperature chart
options.b: Compressor amperage compared against nameplate rated load amps (RLA)
options.c: Superheat at the evaporator and subcooling at the condenser within manufacturer ranges
options.d: Sight glass clarity, with bubbles indicating overcharge of refrigerant

distractorExplanations.a: Suction pressure alone gives saturation temperature but not superheat; charge needs pressure and line temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: Amp draw varies with load and conditions, so it is not a reliable indicator of correct refrigerant charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Bubbles in the sight glass usually indicate undercharge or flash gas, not overcharge.

options.a: Running chillers at full load overnight to cool the building mass before occupancy arrives
options.b: Recirculating indoor air at minimum outdoor air to hold overnight setback
options.c: Flushing warm indoor air and replacing it with cooler outdoor air during unoccupied hours
options.d: Bringing in outdoor air during occupied hours whenever enthalpy is below return

distractorExplanations.a: Mechanical precooling uses chillers; night purge relies on cool outdoor air with fans only.
distractorExplanations.b: Recirculation at minimum outdoor air is normal setback; purge maximizes outdoor air to flush heat.
distractorExplanations.d: Outdoor air cooling during occupied hours is economizer operation; night purge runs during unoccupied hours.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-01.explanation: When nighttime outdoor air is cooler than indoor mass/air, purge ventilation can reduce morning peak cooling load. Purge runs only when outdoor conditions allow.

options.a: Full-load conditions alone, with no part-load rating such as IPLV
options.b: Standardized entering/leaving water temperatures and ambient conditions
options.c: Site-specific design conditions submitted by each manufacturer
options.d: ASHRAE 90.1 climate-zone design temperatures for each project

distractorExplanations.a: AHRI 550/590 defines both full-load ratings and the IPLV/NPLV part-load metrics.
distractorExplanations.c: Manufacturer-chosen site conditions would prevent comparison; AHRI sets standard conditions for everyone.
distractorExplanations.d: ASHRAE 90.1 uses AHRI ratings for its minimum efficiencies but does not define the rating test conditions.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-01.explanation: AHRI conditions normalize chiller performance data so engineers can compare equipment at consistent test points. This gives comparable kW/ton ratings across manufacturers.

options.a: Lower coil capacity because the higher drop raises coil face velocity
options.b: Higher chiller kW/ton because the supply air temperature setpoint must be raised
options.c: Higher fan energy consumption and potential airflow reduction if not compensated
options.d: Higher supply air humidity because the cooling coil bypass factor rises

distractorExplanations.a: Higher filter resistance reduces airflow, which lowers coil face velocity rather than raising it.
distractorExplanations.b: Filter loading affects fan work; it does not force a supply air temperature reset or raise chiller kW/ton.
distractorExplanations.d: Bypass factor depends on coil geometry and face velocity; filter loading mainly increases fan energy.

options.a: Losing conditioned air to unconditioned spaces before it reaches occupied zones
options.b: Drawing unconditioned plenum air into the duct, which raises the supply air temperature
options.c: Raising duct static pressure because leaks add resistance to the supply path
options.d: Overventilating occupied zones as leakage air is counted as outdoor air

distractorExplanations.b: Supply ducts are under positive pressure and leak outward; drawing plenum air inward is return-side leakage.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaks reduce resistance and lower delivered airflow; they do not add resistance to the supply path.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaked supply air never reaches zones, so it does not overventilate them or count as outdoor air.

options.a: Equal pressure drop in every branch by setting all balancing valves fully open
options.b: Design flow rates to coils and terminals so loads are met without excess pump energy
options.c: Maximum velocity in each branch to keep air and debris moving through coils
options.d: Control sequences respond correctly to setpoint changes in each operating mode
