distractorExplanations.a: Fully open valves let near branches take excess flow; balancing sets valves to deliver design flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Excess velocity increases noise, erosion, and pump energy; balancing targets design flow, not maximum velocity.
distractorExplanations.d: Checking sequence response is functional performance testing; hydronic balancing sets design flow rates.

options.a: They use outdoor air for free cooling when conditions are favorable
options.b: They recover heat from exhaust air to precondition the outdoor air supply
options.c: They modulate outdoor air to match occupancy measured by CO2 sensors
options.d: They use condenser water from the tower to make chilled water in winter

distractorExplanations.b: Exhaust heat recovery is an energy recovery requirement in 90.1, not the function of an air economizer.
distractorExplanations.c: Modulating outdoor air by CO2 is demand controlled ventilation, a separate 90.1 provision.
distractorExplanations.d: Making chilled water from tower water is a waterside economizer, which is not an air economizer.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-02.explanation: Economizers can provide significant cooling energy savings where ambient conditions permit. This reduces mechanical cooling energy.

options.a: It replaces designed ventilation, so outdoor air dampers can be closed further
options.b: It raises the building's pressurization, increasing exhaust fan energy
options.c: It increases conduction through walls by lowering their effective R-value
options.d: Unconditioned outdoor air enters the space, adding sensible and latent loads

distractorExplanations.a: Infiltration is uncontrolled and cannot be counted on for ventilation; designed outdoor air is still required.
distractorExplanations.b: Infiltration occurs when the building is at negative pressure relative to outside; it does not pressurize it.
distractorExplanations.c: Conduction depends on R-value, which infiltration does not change; infiltration adds air-exchange loads.

options.a: The fraction of solar radiation incident on the window that is transmitted plus absorbed and reradiated inward
options.b: The fraction of visible light incident on the window that is transmitted through the glazing to the interior
options.c: The rate of heat flow through the window per unit area and degree of indoor-outdoor temperature difference
options.d: The fraction of solar radiation incident on the window that is reflected back outward from the exterior glass surface

distractorExplanations.b: The transmitted fraction of visible light is visible transmittance (VT), not the solar heat gain coefficient.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat flow per unit area per degree of temperature difference is the U-factor, which describes conduction.
distractorExplanations.d: The reflected fraction is solar reflectance; SHGC counts the solar energy that enters the building.

options.a: Localized heat gain only in summer, with no winter condensation concern
options.b: Localized heat loss, condensation risk, and higher peak heating loads
options.c: Air leakage through the parapet cap, which is an air barrier issue
options.d: Uniform loss of R-value across the whole wall area, not a local effect

distractorExplanations.a: Thermal bridges lose heat in winter, creating cold interior spots where condensation can form.
distractorExplanations.c: Air leakage is a separate air barrier problem; thermal bridging is conduction through conductive elements.
distractorExplanations.d: Bridging creates concentrated local heat flow at the detail, not a uniform R-value loss over the wall.

options.a: Serve as the roof's primary air barrier in place of a separate membrane
options.b: Add thermal mass that shifts the roof's peak cooling load to evening
options.c: Raise the roof's solar reflectance so less solar heat is absorbed at the exterior surface
options.d: Reduce thermal bridging through deck fasteners and maintain effective R-value

distractorExplanations.a: Insulation boards are not an air barrier by themselves; the air barrier must be a continuous separate layer.
distractorExplanations.b: Rigid insulation has little thermal mass; its role is resisting heat flow and limiting thermal bridging.
distractorExplanations.c: Solar reflectance is a property of the roof surface or coating, not the insulation layer beneath it.

options.a: Duct leakage to outside, commonly reported as CFM25 per 100 ft²
options.b: Wall thermal resistance, commonly reported as an effective R-value
options.c: Building airtightness, commonly reported as CFM50 or ACH50
options.d: Ventilation airflow at the AHU, commonly reported as outdoor air cfm

distractorExplanations.a: Duct leakage at 25 Pa is measured with a duct blaster test, not a whole-building blower door test.
distractorExplanations.b: Effective R-value comes from calculations or hot-box tests; a blower door measures air leakage.
distractorExplanations.d: Outdoor air cfm at the AHU is measured during TAB; the blower door measures envelope airtightness.

options.a: Heat gains are shifted by storing and releasing heat over time
options.b: Its high R-value stops heat flow so gains do not reach the space
options.c: It reflects solar radiation before the heat reaches the interior
options.d: The building runs 24/7 with no night setback or flushing period

distractorExplanations.b: Mass stores and delays heat; resisting heat flow is the role of insulation R-value, not thermal mass.
distractorExplanations.c: Reflecting solar radiation is a cool roof or glazing property, not the heat storage effect of mass.
distractorExplanations.d: Mass needs a cooler period to discharge stored heat; continuous operation without flushing removes that benefit.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-02.explanation: Mass delays and attenuates peak loads, enabling load shifting strategies in suitable climates and controls. Appropriate ventilation or night flushing is needed to discharge the stored heat.

options.a: Heat loss through the roof in winter
options.b: Conductive heat flow through the roof insulation
options.c: Air leakage through the roof deck seams
options.d: Solar heat absorption by the roof surface

distractorExplanations.a: Cool roofs reduce solar gain, which can slightly increase winter heating; they do not cut winter heat loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Conduction through insulation is governed by R-value; reflectance reduces the solar heat absorbed at the surface.
distractorExplanations.c: Deck seam leakage is an air barrier issue; reflectance does not change air leakage through the roof.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-02.explanation: High reflectance lowers roof surface temperature and heat transfer to the interior, benefiting cooling-dominated buildings. Lower absorption reduces roof surface temperature and cooling load.

options.a: Lower U-factor in winter versus higher solar heat gain in summer
options.b: Reduced solar heat gain versus potential loss of daylight and views
options.c: Higher visible light transmittance versus increased winter heat loss
options.d: Lower glare versus a higher SHGC that raises summer cooling loads

distractorExplanations.a: Solar control films lower SHGC, so they reduce summer solar gain rather than raising it.
distractorExplanations.c: Solar control films generally lower visible transmittance; they do not raise it.
distractorExplanations.d: Solar control films reduce SHGC; a higher SHGC would defeat the purpose of the film.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Films can lower cooling loads but designers must balance visible transmittance, glare, and winter heat gain impacts. The size of the trade-off depends on the film type.

options.a: Air barrier continuity, insulation installation quality, and fenestration performance
options.b: Duct leakage, TAB airflows, and control sequences for each air handler and VAV box
options.c: Roof structural capacity, wind uplift rating, and seismic anchorage
options.d: Daylight sensor calibration, LPD compliance, and exit sign wattage

distractorExplanations.b: Duct leakage, TAB, and sequences are HVAC commissioning scope, not building envelope commissioning.
distractorExplanations.c: Structural capacity and seismic anchorage are verified by the structural engineer, not envelope Cx.
distractorExplanations.d: Daylight sensors and LPD fall under lighting controls commissioning, not envelope commissioning.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Envelope commissioning confirms assemblies perform as intended, supporting accurate loads and durability. Each is checked against the design intent.

options.a: A commanded setpoint value written by the operator to a controller
options.b: A modulating signal sent to a valve or damper actuator by the controller
options.c: A sensor value such as temperature or pressure read by the controller
options.d: An on/off status contact such as a fan proof switch read by the controller

distractorExplanations.a: A writable setpoint is typically an Analog Value (AV) object; AI objects represent physical measured inputs.
distractorExplanations.b: Modulating commands to actuators are Analog Output (AO) objects; AI objects carry measured sensor inputs.
distractorExplanations.d: On/off status contacts are Binary Input (BI) objects; AI objects carry continuously variable measured values.

options.a: Lower first cost than pneumatics in each retrofit, with no added sensors needed
options.b: Elimination of routine calibration because digital sensors do not drift over time
options.c: Faster actuator stroke speeds that let dampers and valves respond within seconds
options.d: Precise software-based control, trending, remote access, and complex sequencing

distractorExplanations.a: DDC retrofits often cost more up front than pneumatic repairs; the driver is control capability and data, not first cost.
distractorExplanations.b: Sensors on digital systems still drift and need periodic calibration; DDC did not remove calibration from O&M programs.
distractorExplanations.c: Actuator speed is a hardware property shared by pneumatic and electric actuators; DDC's advantage is software logic and trending.

options.a: Continuously adjust outputs to minimize error between setpoint and measured process variable
options.b: Switch outputs fully on or off when the variable crosses a fixed differential band
options.c: Schedule equipment start and stop times based on occupancy calendars and holidays
options.d: Step outputs up or down on a fixed outdoor-temperature schedule without measuring the zone variable

distractorExplanations.b: Switching fully on/off around a differential describes two-position (on/off) control, not PID modulation.
distractorExplanations.c: Occupancy start/stop is a time-of-day scheduling function, not a closed-loop PID algorithm acting on error.
distractorExplanations.d: Acting on outdoor temperature without feedback from the controlled variable is open-loop control; PID needs measured feedback.

options.a: Starts HVAC at a fixed time each morning chosen from the coldest design day
options.b: Calculates the latest start and earliest stop times to meet occupancy comfort
options.c: Calculates the earliest start and latest stop times to maximize comfort margins
options.d: Runs equipment at reduced capacity overnight so no morning warm-up is required

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed start time sized for the design day is conventional scheduling; optimal start varies the start time daily from conditions.
distractorExplanations.c: Earliest start and latest stop maximize runtime; optimal start/stop does the opposite, using the latest start and earliest stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding reduced capacity overnight is a standby strategy that adds runtime hours; optimal start removes unneeded hours.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Optimal algorithms reduce runtime while ensuring space conditions are met at occupancy. The timing is based on learned building response.

options.a: Running the most efficient available chiller(s) at favorable load points
options.b: Staging chillers on equal runtime hours first, with efficiency as a tiebreaker
options.c: Bringing on the next chiller as soon as the lead machine reaches 50% load
options.d: Running the largest chiller first so that one machine can carry most loads

distractorExplanations.b: Runtime equalization is a maintenance goal; letting it override efficiency puts less efficient machines online at poor load points.
distractorExplanations.c: Staging up at 50% runs two machines lightly loaded; staging should follow where each chiller's kW/ton is best, often at higher loads.
distractorExplanations.d: The largest chiller is not necessarily the most efficient at the actual load; an oversized lead machine runs at low part load.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Effective staging matches capacity to load and selects efficient combinations, considering lift and part-load performance. Good sequencing also minimizes simultaneous inefficient operation.

options.a: Routing every alarm to the same email list so that no notification is missed
options.b: Setting alarm limits at the equipment design ratings so alarms rarely occur
options.c: Prioritization, nuisance alarm reduction, and documented response procedures
options.d: Assigning critical priority to temperature alarms so operators respond fastest

distractorExplanations.a: Sending every alarm to one list without priority creates alarm fatigue; operators need severity tiers and routing by role.
distractorExplanations.b: Limits set at design ratings flag faults too late; energy-waste alarms need tighter, operationally meaningful thresholds.
distractorExplanations.d: Elevating routine temperature alarms to critical dilutes true life-safety and equipment-failure alarms; priorities must be tiered.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Actionable alarms with clear severity help operators maintain performance without alarm fatigue. Response procedures should be written for operators.

options.a: Envelope air leakage locations that need blower-door testing and air sealing
options.b: Design airflow and capacity shortfalls that require replacing the equipment
options.c: Utility billing errors such as wrong rate schedules or meter multiplier mistakes
options.d: Control problems such as simultaneous heating and cooling or hunting valves

distractorExplanations.a: Leakage locations come from blower-door and infrared testing; BAS trends show control behavior, not where the envelope leaks.
distractorExplanations.b: Trend reviews in RCx mostly reveal operational and sequence problems fixable at low cost, not capacity shortfalls needing replacement.
distractorExplanations.c: Billing errors are found by bill audits against the tariff; BAS trend logs record equipment points, not utility rates or multipliers.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-03.explanation: Long-term trend data shows how systems actually operate versus design intent. Economizers locked out are another common finding.

options.a: Increases reheat energy because zones drift farther from setpoint
options.b: Reduces simultaneous heating and cooling when properly enforced
options.c: Raises fan energy because supply airflow must rise to hold comfort
options.d: Mainly lowers peak demand by staggering heating and cooling starts

distractorExplanations.a: Drifting within the deadband means neither heating nor cooling runs; reheat drops rather than rises with a wider deadband.
distractorExplanations.c: In the deadband VAV boxes sit at minimum airflow; a wider deadband lowers rather than raises fan and reheat energy.
distractorExplanations.d: Deadband targets concurrent heating and cooling energy in a zone; staggering equipment starts is a separate demand-limiting tactic.

options.a: Raise outdoor air to purge the zone each time the sensor detects vacancy
options.b: Hold full ventilation in unoccupied zones and reset space temperature alone
options.c: Reduce ventilation, lighting, or conditioning in unoccupied zones
options.d: Shut off zone exhaust fans while keeping lighting on for security reasons

distractorExplanations.a: Vacancy should cut outdoor air toward the occupied-standby minimum; purging on every vacancy wastes conditioning energy.
distractorExplanations.b: Codes such as ASHRAE 90.1 allow ventilation to drop in vacant zones; resetting temperature alone leaves ventilation savings unused.
distractorExplanations.d: Occupancy integration typically turns lighting off in vacant zones; cutting exhaust while leaving lights on reverses the intent.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: Occupancy-based control saves energy when sequences respect life safety and ventilation minimums. Reductions must follow the control sequence and code limits.

options.a: Optimize setpoints continuously by writing new values to field controllers in real time
options.b: Identify equipment or control faults early using rules or analytics on operational data
options.c: Verify savings for each ECM against an adjusted baseline using IPMVP Option B
options.d: Schedule preventive maintenance tasks at fixed intervals from equipment run hours

distractorExplanations.a: Writing optimized setpoints is supervisory optimization control; FDD detects and diagnoses faults, often without commanding.
distractorExplanations.c: Savings verification against a baseline is M&V; FDD diagnoses faults such as stuck dampers or sensor drift in operating data.
distractorExplanations.d: Run-hour PM scheduling is a CMMS function; FDD uses operational data to flag faults as they appear, enabling condition-based work.

options.a: Merging BAS controllers onto the corporate office LAN so that IT tools can monitor them directly
options.b: Allowing vendor remote access through a shared account with a strong password
options.c: Deferring controller firmware updates until equipment replacement to avoid any operational downtime
options.d: Segmenting control networks from general IT and restricting remote access with authentication

distractorExplanations.a: Flattening the BAS onto the office LAN widens the attack surface; segmentation keeps control traffic isolated from general IT.
distractorExplanations.b: A shared vendor account, even with a strong password, prevents individual accountability; each user needs unique authenticated access.
distractorExplanations.c: Deferring patches leaves known vulnerabilities open for years; updates should be scheduled and tested, not postponed to replacement.

options.a: Determine each end use's exact share of consumption without any submetering
options.b: Replace the utility revenue meter reading in billing disputes with BAS totals
options.c: Correlate whole-building consumption with equipment operation and identify anomalies
options.d: Set the utility demand ratchet level by forecasting next month's peak from the BAS trend data

distractorExplanations.a: Whole-building interval data cannot disaggregate end uses exactly; submeters or engineering estimates are still needed for detail.
distractorExplanations.b: BAS trend points are not revenue-grade; billing disputes rely on utility or shadow revenue meters, not controller totals.
distractorExplanations.d: Ratchet levels are set by the tariff from recorded billing peaks; customers cannot set them from their own BAS forecasts.

options.a: It focuses on existing systems using operational data to find drift from design or changed use
options.b: It is performed before occupancy to confirm the design intent of new systems
options.c: It re-commissions a building that was already commissioned, repeating the process on a periodic cycle
options.d: It replaces aging equipment with new high-efficiency units sized to the building's current loads

distractorExplanations.b: Pre-occupancy verification of design intent describes initial (new-building) commissioning, the opposite of retrocommissioning.
distractorExplanations.c: Periodic repeat of a previously commissioned building is re-commissioning; RCx is a first commissioning of an existing building.
distractorExplanations.d: Equipment replacement is a capital retrofit; RCx focuses on low-cost operational fixes to existing systems and controls.

options.a: Rotating lead and lag chillers to balance runtime across machines
options.b: Multiple chillers operating at very low part load simultaneously
options.c: Resetting condenser water temperature lower when wet-bulb allows
options.d: Locking out a chiller when load falls below its minimum stable flow

distractorExplanations.a: Lead/lag rotation balances wear and is a sound practice; parallel chiller sequences should keep it, not avoid it.
distractorExplanations.c: Lowering condenser water temperature when wet-bulb permits reduces lift and kW/ton; it is a recommended strategy.
distractorExplanations.d: Lockout below minimum stable flow protects the machine from surge and low-flow trips; it should be included, not avoided.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: Poor staging increases kW/ton by running too many machines at inefficient low loads. This matters most when one chiller could carry the load efficiently.

options.a: Tuning excess air, maintaining clean heat transfer surfaces, and recovering waste heat
options.b: Raising excess air well above 30% to ensure complete burnout at each firing rate
options.c: Raising stack temperature so that more heat leaves with the flue gas as useful work
options.d: Increasing blowdown frequency and firing at maximum steam pressure in each season

distractorExplanations.b: Excess air far above the burner's optimum carries heat up the stack; typical gas targets are about 10-15% (2-3% O2).
distractorExplanations.c: Higher stack temperature means more heat lost to the flue; efficiency improves when stack temperature is lowered.
distractorExplanations.d: Extra blowdown discards heated water and needless high pressure raises losses; neither improves combustion efficiency.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Efficient combustion minimizes excess air while maintaining complete burn and maximizing heat transfer to the load. Waste heat recovery applies where feasible.

options.a: Hold a fixed air damper position set during the annual tune-up
options.b: Maintain target carbon dioxide in the combustion air across loads
options.c: Maintain target excess oxygen in the flue gas across varying loads
options.d: Maintain a target stack temperature by modulating the feedwater pump

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed damper position is mechanical linkage control without feedback; O2 trim corrects air based on measured flue oxygen.
distractorExplanations.b: Trim measures oxygen (or CO) in the flue gas, not CO2 in incoming combustion air, which is essentially ambient air.
distractorExplanations.d: Feedwater control maintains drum level; O2 trim adjusts the air-fuel ratio, and stack temperature is a result, not its setpoint.

options.a: Returning blowdown water to the deaerator as clean feedwater makeup
options.b: Reducing the blowdown rate by raising boiler water conductivity limits
options.c: Capturing latent heat from flue gas condensing in the economizer section of the stack
options.d: Capturing sensible heat from blowdown water before it is discharged to drain

distractorExplanations.a: Blowdown carries concentrated dissolved solids; returning it as feedwater defeats its purpose. Only its heat and flash steam are reused.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing conductivity limits adjusts how much blowdown occurs; blowdown heat recovery captures heat from whatever is discharged.
distractorExplanations.c: Flue-gas condensing recovery is a condensing economizer measure, not blowdown heat recovery from boiler water.

options.a: Condensate backing up into heat exchangers when traps fail open
options.b: Live steam loss to condensate return or atmosphere, wasting fuel
options.c: Higher steam pressure in the mains as failed traps hold back steam
options.d: Lower boiler load because less condensate is returned to the plant

distractorExplanations.a: Traps failing open blow live steam through; condensate backup into equipment is the symptom of a trap that fails closed.
distractorExplanations.c: Failed-open traps vent steam and lower available pressure; they do not raise main pressure by holding steam back.
distractorExplanations.d: Steam lost through failed traps must be replaced by the boiler, raising fuel use and makeup water rather than lowering load.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Blown traps pass steam continuously, increasing boiler load and risking system damage. Failed traps can also cause water hammer.

options.a: Returned condensate retains heat and reduces makeup water heating demand
options.b: Returned condensate raises boiler pressure and lowers the firing rate
options.c: Returned condensate needs no deaeration, removing deaerator steam use
options.d: Returned condensate contains latent heat that is released in the boiler

distractorExplanations.b: Condensate return affects feedwater temperature, not operating pressure; the fuel saving comes from heat already in the water.
distractorExplanations.c: Condensate still passes through the deaerator; return mainly cuts makeup heating, treatment chemicals, and water costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Condensate has already given up its latent heat at the process; what it returns is sensible heat that preheats feedwater.

options.a: The ratio of steam output to fuel input at full firing rate
options.b: The time needed to go from cold start to full firing rate
options.c: The share of boiler capacity held in reserve at peak load
options.d: The range between minimum and maximum stable firing rate

distractorExplanations.a: Output divided by fuel input is boiler efficiency; turndown compares the maximum to the minimum stable firing rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Cold-start time is a warm-up or ramp-rate characteristic; turndown is the max-to-min stable firing rate ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: Reserve capacity at peak is a redundancy or standby margin, not the burner's maximum-to-minimum firing ratio.

options.a: Compressors consume significant electricity to produce air that performs no useful work
options.b: Leaks lower system pressure, which mainly raises the risk of compressed air dryer freeze-ups
options.c: Leak losses are mostly a water-treatment cost from the extra condensate drainage they create
options.d: Leaks add demand charges but use no extra kWh because compressors run anyway

distractorExplanations.b: Leak pressure drop affects end-use tools and compressor runtime; dryer freezing is not the main cost of leaks.
distractorExplanations.c: Condensate drainage is minor; the dominant cost of leaks is the compressor electricity used to make air that is wasted.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaks add compressor runtime and kWh as well as demand; compressors run longer and load more to replace leaked air.

options.a: Lower pressure raises air density at the compressor inlet and boosts output
options.b: Lower pressure lets end-use tools run faster, shortening process cycle times
options.c: Compressor power decreases when less pressure rise is required for the same flow
options.d: Compressor motor efficiency rises sharply at lower discharge pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Inlet density depends on ambient conditions, not system discharge pressure; savings come from a lower compression ratio.
distractorExplanations.b: Tools at lower pressure typically deliver less force or speed; the saving comes from compressor power, not faster tools.
distractorExplanations.d: Motor efficiency is nearly flat across normal loads; savings come from less compression work, not a jump in motor efficiency.

options.a: Ranking exhaust streams by volume flow rate without regard to temperature
options.b: Targeting exhaust streams above 1,000°F because lower grades are unusable
options.c: Surveying electrical submeters to find motors with the highest run hours
options.d: Mapping energy flows and finding exhaust streams with usable temperature

distractorExplanations.a: Recoverable heat depends on temperature and heat capacity relative to sinks; flow rate alone does not identify usable heat.
distractorExplanations.b: Low- and medium-grade waste heat (below about 450°F) is widely recovered for preheating water, air, and process streams.
distractorExplanations.c: Motor run-hour surveys find drive and motor opportunities; heat recovery requires thermal stream temperatures and loads.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Pinch analysis and heat balances reveal where recovered heat can preheat combustion air, water, or process loads. The usable temperature must sit above downstream needs.

options.a: Generating power at higher electrical efficiency than a combined-cycle plant
options.b: Running the prime mover at grid peak hours to export power to the utility
options.c: Using utility power for thermal loads and onsite fuel for electrical loads
options.d: Using waste heat from power generation for thermal loads instead of rejecting it

distractorExplanations.a: CHP prime movers usually have lower electrical efficiency than combined-cycle plants; the gain comes from using the heat.
distractorExplanations.b: Peak export is a dispatch strategy; CHP's fuel-utilization gain depends on using recovered heat at a thermal load.
distractorExplanations.c: This swaps energy sources without capturing waste heat; CHP generates power onsite and recovers its rejected heat.

options.a: Lowering fluid velocity so that heat exchangers reach a smaller approach
options.b: Raising the overall U-value because deposits add surface area for transfer
options.c: Adding thermal resistance and requiring higher approach temperatures or flow
options.d: Lowering pump head, which forces control valves to throttle and waste energy

distractorExplanations.a: Fouling narrows passages, raising pressure drop, and widens the approach; it does not produce a smaller approach.
distractorExplanations.b: Deposits add a fouling resistance that lowers the overall U-value; any added area is negligible versus the resistance.
distractorExplanations.d: Fouling raises, not lowers, pressure drop and pump head; extra pumping energy comes from that higher resistance.

options.a: Motors operate most efficiently near full load; low load factor may indicate oversizing
options.b: Motors operate most efficiently near 25% load; high load factor indicates overloading
options.c: Load factor sets the motor's utility demand charge independent of its runtime
options.d: Low load factor means a motor has a high power factor and needs no correction

distractorExplanations.b: Motor efficiency peaks roughly at 75-100% load and drops sharply below about 40%; 25% load is inefficient operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Demand charges depend on coincident peak kW; load factor describes average versus rated motor load for efficiency screening.
distractorExplanations.d: Lightly loaded induction motors have low, not high, power factor; low load factor often worsens reactive demand.

options.a: Lower pressure raises steam's saturation temperature and speeds heat transfer
options.b: Lower pressure steam has less latent heat, so each pound carries less energy
options.c: Lower pressure eliminates flash steam at condensate traps and receivers
options.d: Lower pressure reduces heat loss through piping and may improve boiler efficiency

distractorExplanations.a: Saturation temperature falls as pressure drops; the heat transfer driving force decreases, which is why process needs set the floor.
distractorExplanations.b: Latent heat per pound actually rises slightly as pressure falls; the saving comes from lower line and flash losses.
distractorExplanations.c: Flash steam forms whenever condensate drops to a lower pressure; lowering system pressure reduces flash rather than eliminating it.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Lower system pressure reduces saturation temperature and line losses if process requirements permit. The boiler efficiency gain comes at lower firing.

options.a: Excess air and incomplete combustion that raise flue-gas stack losses
options.b: Soot buildup on fireside tube surfaces that raises the stack temperature
options.c: Scale, corrosion, and carryover that reduce efficiency and damage equipment
options.d: Steam trap failures and condensate line leaks across the distribution system

distractorExplanations.a: Excess air is a fireside combustion issue controlled by tuning and O2 trim; water treatment protects the waterside.
distractorExplanations.b: Fireside soot comes from combustion and is cleaned by soot blowing or tuning; water treatment addresses waterside scale.
distractorExplanations.d: Trap failures are mechanical issues found by trap surveys; treatment controls waterside chemistry, though it slows line corrosion.

options.a: Actual energy output divided by theoretical maximum output at rated capacity over a period
options.b: Actual AC energy output divided by the total solar energy incident on the module surface
options.c: Peak sun hours per day divided by 24 hours, adjusted for the inverter rating
options.d: Measured output divided by modeled expected output for the same weather period, as a percentage

distractorExplanations.b: Output divided by incident solar energy is system or module conversion efficiency, not capacity factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Peak sun hours describe the solar resource; capacity factor compares actual kWh to rated kW times hours in the period.
distractorExplanations.d: Measured versus modeled output under actual weather is the performance ratio or performance index, not capacity factor.

options.a: Rated power, rotor diameter, and grid voltage level
options.b: Tower height alone, since wind speed rises with height
options.c: Turbine nameplate rating and the local electric tariff
options.d: Wind resource, turbine availability, and wake losses

distractorExplanations.a: Rated power is the denominator of capacity factor; grid voltage does not determine how much of it the site achieves.
distractorExplanations.b: Hub height matters through the wind resource, but availability and wake losses also drive capacity factor; height alone is incomplete.
distractorExplanations.c: Tariffs affect project revenue, not physical energy production; capacity factor depends on resource, availability, and losses.

options.a: Process needs low- to medium-temperature heat and good solar resource with storage or backup
options.b: Process needs high-pressure steam above 400°F with demand peaking during the night shifts
options.c: Process load runs mainly on night shifts and the site lacks any thermal storage for solar heat
options.d: Process heat is supplied by cheap waste heat already available onsite

distractorExplanations.b: Typical flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors serve low to medium temperatures; night peaks also mismatch solar supply.
distractorExplanations.c: Solar collection occurs in daylight; night-dominant loads without storage leave collected heat unused.
distractorExplanations.d: Free waste heat already onsite undercuts solar thermal economics; solar preheat fits where fossil preheat would otherwise be bought.

options.a: Water chemistry and blowdown alone, since combustion runs much like natural gas
options.b: Electrical service sizing and harmonics from the boiler's heating elements
options.c: Refrigerant charge, compressor lift, and condenser fouling in the heat loop
options.d: Fuel supply consistency, emissions controls, ash handling, and combustion tuning

distractorExplanations.a: Biomass combustion differs from gas firing: variable fuel moisture and size require fuel handling, ash removal, and tuning.
distractorExplanations.b: Heating elements and harmonics belong to electric boilers; biomass units burn solid fuel and need fuel and ash systems.
distractorExplanations.c: Refrigerant charge and lift are heat pump or chiller concerns; biomass boilers raise heat by combustion, not compression.

options.a: Electrochemical reaction, often with usable heat depending on type
options.b: Combustion of hydrogen in a micro-turbine that drives a small generator
options.c: Photovoltaic conversion of light in cells stacked inside a sealed module
options.d: Thermoelectric conversion of a temperature difference across a junction

distractorExplanations.b: Fuel cells convert fuel chemically without combustion; burning fuel in a micro-turbine is a different DG technology.
distractorExplanations.c: Light-to-electricity conversion is photovoltaics; fuel cells use an electrochemical reaction of hydrogen-rich fuel and oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: Thermoelectric generators use the Seebeck effect across a junction; fuel cells react fuel and oxidant at electrodes.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Fuel cells offer high electrical efficiency and recoverable heat for CHP applications. High-temperature types such as MCFC and SOFC offer the most usable heat.

options.a: The local system trips its generators offline whenever the utility grid is lost and waits for restoration
options.b: The local system exports surplus generation to the grid during peak hours
options.c: The local system can disconnect from the utility grid and continue serving critical loads
options.d: The local system runs permanently off-grid with no utility interconnection or parallel operation

distractorExplanations.a: Shutting down on grid loss is standard anti-islanding behavior for grid-tied inverters; islanding keeps serving loads.
distractorExplanations.b: Exporting surplus is grid-parallel operation under net metering or export rules; islanding means operating disconnected.
distractorExplanations.d: A permanently off-grid system is not a microgrid with islanding capability, which connects and disconnects as needed.

options.a: A tradable permit for one ton of CO2 emitted under a cap-and-trade program
options.b: Physical delivery of renewable electrons from a named generator to the site
options.c: A verified emission reduction credit from a project like methane capture
options.d: The environmental attributes of renewable generation, separable from energy

distractorExplanations.a: Emission allowances under cap-and-trade are a different instrument; one REC represents 1 MWh of renewable generation attributes.
distractorExplanations.b: Electrons on a shared grid cannot be traced; RECs track attribute ownership separate from the physical power flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Project-based carbon offsets measure tonnes of avoided emissions; RECs certify MWh of renewable generation attributes.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: RECs document renewable attribute claims for compliance or voluntary goals. Separation from the energy applies in some markets.

options.a: The site's ECM savings potential and its eligibility for utility rebates
options.b: Grid impacts, protection settings, and power quality for safe parallel operation
options.c: Generator fuel supply contracts and onsite emissions permit conditions for the new unit
options.d: Building load profiles to size the generator for maximum self-consumption

distractorExplanations.a: Savings potential and rebates come from audits and program rules; interconnection studies assess grid safety and reliability.
distractorExplanations.c: Fuel contracts and air permits are separate project tasks; utilities study fault current, protection, and power quality.
distractorExplanations.d: Load profiles inform the owner's sizing decision; the utility study evaluates impacts on the distribution system.

options.a: Feedwater or combustion air using flue gas heat before it exits the stack
options.b: Makeup water using heat recovered from continuous surface blowdown before the deaerator
options.c: Outdoor ventilation air using exhaust air from the boiler room
options.d: Condensate return using flash steam from the deaerator vent

distractorExplanations.b: Preheating makeup with blowdown heat is a blowdown heat exchanger, not an economizer, which uses flue gas heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Exhaust-to-ventilation air recovery is an HVAC energy recovery ventilator; an economizer recovers flue gas heat.
distractorExplanations.d: Flash steam and vent condensers recover deaerator or condensate heat; economizers transfer stack heat to feedwater.

options.a: Lowering steam velocity so less pressure drop occurs in the mains
options.b: Lowering heat transfer from hot pipes to ambient surroundings
options.c: Raising steam pressure so condensate forms farther from the boiler
options.d: Lowering the steam's saturation temperature to cut surface losses

distractorExplanations.a: Velocity and pressure drop depend on pipe size and flow; insulation reduces heat loss, not friction in the mains.
distractorExplanations.c: Insulation does not change system pressure; it reduces condensation caused by heat loss along the line.
distractorExplanations.d: Saturation temperature is set by pressure, not insulation; insulation adds thermal resistance between the pipe and air.

options.a: The difference between peak and off-peak electricity prices in a TOU tariff
options.b: The ratio of electrical output to fuel input of the CHP prime mover
options.c: The difference between natural gas commodity and pipeline delivery charges
options.d: The difference between electricity purchase price and fuel cost

distractorExplanations.a: The peak/off-peak spread drives load shifting and storage; spark spread compares the power price with the fuel cost.
distractorExplanations.b: Output over fuel input is electrical efficiency; spark spread is a price difference between electricity and fuel.
distractorExplanations.c: Commodity versus delivery split is a gas bill structure; spark spread compares electricity price against fuel cost.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Favorable spark spread means onsite generation fuel cost is below avoided electricity cost. The comparison is made on an equivalent energy basis.

options.a: There is a large winter heating load and little summer cooling demand
options.b: Electricity is cheap relative to gas and recovered heat is unavailable
options.c: Recovered heat is available only at 120°F from engine jacket water
options.d: There is sufficient thermal input and concurrent cooling load

distractorExplanations.a: Absorption chillers need a cooling load; a heating-dominated site would use CHP heat directly, not for cooling.
distractorExplanations.b: Cheap power and no waste heat favor electric chillers; absorption pays off when recovered heat is free and power costly.
distractorExplanations.c: Single-effect absorbers need hot water around 180-200°F or steam; 120°F heat is too low to drive them well.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Heat-driven cooling leverages CHP thermal output, improving overall system efficiency. Both conditions are needed to utilize the recovered heat.

options.a: Throttled valves, oversized pumps, and poor maintenance of impellers and seals
options.b: Undersized pumps that run continuously at the right end of their curves
options.c: VFD-controlled pumps with trimmed impellers matched to the system curve
options.d: Low-friction piping layouts that let pumps run near best efficiency point

distractorExplanations.b: Oversizing, not undersizing, is the common waste; oversized pumps are throttled back and run far from best efficiency.
distractorExplanations.c: VFDs and impeller trimming are remedies that cut pumping energy, not typical sources of waste.
distractorExplanations.d: Running near BEP with low friction is the efficient condition; waste comes from throttling and pump-system mismatch.

options.a: Demand is steady at full load and the compressor rarely unloads
options.b: Demand varies and inlet modulation or unload modes would otherwise waste power
options.c: Demand varies but the VFD unit serves as a constant base-load machine
options.d: Demand is steady and the plant pressure setpoint is raised to cover occasional peaks

distractorExplanations.a: At steady full load a fixed-speed compressor runs efficiently; a VFD adds drive losses and gives little benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: A VFD compressor should be the trim unit; running it as base load at full speed wastes its part-load advantage.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising pressure increases compressor power and leak flow; a VFD's benefit comes from varying demand, not higher setpoints.

options.a: The lowest flue gas temperature allowed before acid condensation occurs in the stack
options.b: The economic pipe size that balances friction loss against first cost
options.c: The point of maximum heat exchanger effectiveness in a single counterflow exchanger unit
options.d: The minimum temperature approach limiting heat recovery between hot and cold streams

distractorExplanations.a: That is the acid dew point limit on stack heat recovery; pinch analysis finds the network temperature bottleneck.
distractorExplanations.b: Economic pipe sizing trades pumping energy against capital cost; pinch analysis concerns heat exchange between streams.
distractorExplanations.c: Effectiveness describes a single exchanger; pinch analysis uses composite curves for the whole process network.

options.a: Increases output in the first years as cells cure, then levels off
options.b: Reduces output gradually due to cell aging and potential-induced degradation
options.c: Reduces output by about 5% per year until the warranty period ends
options.d: Lowers inverter efficiency each year while module output stays at STC rating

distractorExplanations.a: Modules lose output early through light-induced degradation rather than gaining; output then declines about 0.5%/year.
distractorExplanations.c: Typical degradation is about 0.5-0.8% per year; 5% per year would exceed standard performance warranties many times over.
distractorExplanations.d: Degradation refers to module power loss; inverter efficiency is a separate component rating that degradation rates do not describe.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Financial models use degradation rates (often ~0.5%/year) for long-term production estimates. Soiling adds further output losses in the field.

options.a: DC array maximum power exceeds inverter AC rating and output is limited at peak sun
options.b: AC grid voltage drops below the inverter's minimum setting and output trips offline briefly
options.c: Module temperature rises at peak sun and lowers the array's voltage output
options.d: Shading of one string forces bypass diodes to cut that string's output

distractorExplanations.b: Low grid voltage causes an under-voltage trip, which stops output; clipping is a power limit with output continuing.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat-related voltage loss is temperature derating of modules; clipping happens at the inverter's AC power limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Bypass diode activation is a shading mismatch loss; clipping occurs when DC power exceeds the inverter AC rating.

options.a: Loop fluid has higher glycol concentration than freeze protection needs
options.b: Entering source temperature is favorable relative to required lift
options.c: Loop flow rate is reduced to cut pumping energy below design minimum
options.d: Supply water temperature to the building is raised in heating mode

distractorExplanations.a: Excess glycol raises viscosity and pumping energy and lowers heat transfer, reducing rather than improving COP.
distractorExplanations.c: Flow below design raises the temperature change across the heat pump, increasing lift and possibly tripping units.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher heating supply temperature increases compressor lift and lowers COP; lower supply temperatures improve it.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Stable ground temperatures reduce lift compared to air-source extremes, improving COP. This applies in both heating and cooling mode.

options.a: Gas is compressed to the burner supply pressure without removing H2S or moisture
options.b: Gas methane content is held below 30% so that flame temperatures stay low
options.c: Gas is cleaned to meet equipment fuel specifications and heating value is sufficient
options.d: Gas is blended with air before storage to raise its heating value per cubic foot

distractorExplanations.a: Compression alone leaves H2S, moisture, and siloxanes that corrode and foul engines and boilers; cleaning is required.
distractorExplanations.b: Digester gas typically runs 55-65% methane; very low methane makes combustion unstable and reduces heating value.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding air dilutes heating value and can create explosive mixtures; heating value rises by removing CO2, not adding air.

options.a: Run at maximum boiler design pressure so that steam carries more energy
options.b: Match the lowest pressure adequate for all connected loads to minimize losses
options.c: Be set by the average pressure demand of connected loads rather than the highest need
options.d: Stay at boiler pressure with each user throttling steam by hand valves

distractorExplanations.a: Higher pressure raises line, flash, and trap losses; latent heat per pound actually falls as pressure rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Setting to the average starves the most demanding loads; header pressure must satisfy the highest required use pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand throttling wastes control and causes erratic supply; PRVs or separate headers step pressure down to each use point.

options.a: The boiler frequently short-cycles at low load without turndown or buffer capacity
options.b: The boiler runs continuously at high fire to carry a steady process base load
options.c: Several smaller modular boilers are staged in sequence to follow load swings
options.d: The burner has a high turndown ratio and modulates down at light loads

distractorExplanations.b: Continuous steady firing minimizes purge and standby losses; cycling losses arise from frequent on/off operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Staging smaller modules matches load and reduces cycling; it is a remedy, not a cause of cycling losses.
distractorExplanations.d: High turndown lets the burner modulate rather than cycle, lowering losses; low turndown is what causes short cycling.

options.a: Calculate combustion efficiency directly from the hourly steam flow data
options.b: Size the boiler plant for the annual average load to reduce standby losses
options.c: Set the water treatment chemical feed rate from the daily peak firing rate
options.d: Identify opportunities for scheduling, staging, and right-sizing equipment

distractorExplanations.a: Combustion efficiency needs flue O2 and stack temperature; steam flow profiles show load timing and part-load hours.
distractorExplanations.b: Sizing to the average load leaves peaks unmet; profiling supports right-sizing to actual peaks and part-load hours.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical feed is set from makeup volume and water chemistry tests, not from load profiling of peak firing.

options.a: The site finances and owns the system through a loan repaid from savings
options.b: A third party owns and operates the system while the site buys energy at agreed rates
options.c: The site leases the equipment for a fixed monthly fee independent of output
options.d: The utility owns the array on site and credits the customer at the retail net-metering rate

distractorExplanations.a: Owner financing through a loan is direct ownership; under a PPA a third party owns the system and sells the power.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed lease payment not tied to output is a solar lease; a PPA bills per kWh actually produced.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility-owned arrays with bill credits describe community or utility solar programs; PPAs use a third-party developer.

options.a: Fuel carbon content, generation efficiency, and displaced grid emissions factors
options.b: Fuel carbon content alone, since displaced grid power is treated as having no emissions
options.c: Generator nameplate kW and annual run hours, without any fuel or grid emissions data
options.d: Grid emissions factors and onsite peak demand, with fuel use excluded

distractorExplanations.b: Displaced grid electricity carries an emissions factor; omitting it misstates DG's net emissions impact.
distractorExplanations.c: Nameplate and hours give energy output but not emissions; fuel carbon content and efficiency set DG emissions.
distractorExplanations.d: Excluding DG fuel use ignores the onsite source of emissions; net impact compares DG fuel emissions with grid emissions.

options.a: Traps that are blowing live steam or blocked by distinguishing acoustic signatures
options.b: Trap body surface temperature, to confirm the condensate is subcooled below 100°F at discharge
options.c: Wall thickness loss in steam mains caused by erosion and corrosion
options.d: Dissolved oxygen levels in the condensate returning from the traps to the deaerator

distractorExplanations.b: Surface temperature is measured with infrared or contact thermometers; ultrasound detects flow noise through the trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Pipe wall thickness is measured by ultrasonic thickness gauging, a different technique from acoustic trap testing.
distractorExplanations.d: Dissolved oxygen is measured by water chemistry sampling; ultrasonic trap testing listens for steam or condensate flow.

options.a: Hold blowdown at a fixed 10% of steam flow set at commissioning
options.b: Maximize cycles of concentration even beyond conductivity limits
options.c: Maintain acceptable water chemistry while minimizing energy loss
options.d: Minimize energy loss by blowing down once per shift by hand

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed blowdown rate ignores changing makeup quality; the rate should follow measured conductivity or TDS.
distractorExplanations.b: Exceeding conductivity limits causes scale and carryover; cycles should be raised only up to the chemistry limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Infrequent manual blowdown lets TDS swing above and below targets; continuous conductivity control is better.

options.a: Produces steam by burning fuel in a fired furnace with no exhaust input
options.b: Condenses turbine exhaust steam and returns it as boiler feedwater
options.c: Produces chilled water from exhaust heat using a lithium bromide cycle
options.d: Produces steam from exhaust heat of a gas turbine or reciprocating engine

distractorExplanations.a: A conventional fired boiler burns fuel directly; an HRSG uses prime-mover exhaust, with duct burners only supplementing.
distractorExplanations.b: Condensing exhaust steam is the job of a surface condenser; an HRSG generates steam from hot exhaust gas.
distractorExplanations.c: Exhaust-driven chilled water comes from an absorption chiller; an HRSG produces steam or hot water, not chilled water.

options.a: Lower cooling tower load for absorption chillers versus higher load for electric units
options.b: Heat input versus electrical kW/ton depending on relative fuel and power costs
options.c: Higher COP for absorption versus lower COP for electric chillers
options.d: Electric demand charges versus chiller refrigerant phase-out risk

distractorExplanations.a: Absorption chillers reject more heat per ton than electric chillers, so they need larger, not smaller, cooling towers.
distractorExplanations.c: Absorption COPs run about 0.7-1.4, well below electric chillers' COP of 5-7; the trade is energy source and cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Refrigerant phase-out is a secondary factor; the core trade-off is thermal input cost versus electric kW/ton.

options.a: Flue gas or process heat to raise incoming air temperature before the burner
options.b: Flue gas heat to raise feedwater temperature before the boiler drum
options.c: Blowdown heat to warm makeup water before it enters the deaerator
options.d: Steam coils to warm the boiler room so combustion air stays above freezing

distractorExplanations.b: Heating feedwater with flue gas is an economizer function; combustion air preheat heats the burner's air supply.
distractorExplanations.c: Blowdown heat recovery preheats makeup water; combustion air preheaters heat the air going to the burner.
distractorExplanations.d: Steam-heated room air uses boiler output rather than recovering waste heat, so it does not save fuel.

options.a: Faces due west at a tilt near latitude to maximize annual energy yield
options.b: Faces south (or north in southern hemisphere) at tilt near latitude
options.c: Faces south at a tilt near latitude plus 15° to maximize summer output
options.d: Faces north at a tilt near latitude to reduce module heating losses

distractorExplanations.a: West orientation shifts output to afternoon peaks but lowers annual yield versus south in the northern hemisphere.
distractorExplanations.c: Latitude plus about 15° favors winter output; summer optimization uses a tilt lower than latitude.
distractorExplanations.d: North-facing arrays in the northern hemisphere lose substantial irradiance; cooler modules do not offset it.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Site-specific modeling accounts for latitude, tariff, and shading for optimal yield. This orientation maximizes annual energy.

options.a: Seasonal storage that shifts summer solar output to winter heating
options.b: Power factor correction that replaces the need for utility interconnection studies
options.c: Reduction of annual kWh consumption through round-trip efficiency gains
options.d: Peak shaving, backup power, and arbitrage where economics and controls support it

distractorExplanations.a: Batteries store hours, not months; seasonal shifting is beyond typical lithium-ion economics and duration.
distractorExplanations.b: Storage inverters can supply reactive power, but storage still requires interconnection review and protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Round-trip losses of about 10-15% increase total kWh; storage saves on timing and demand, not consumption.

options.a: Compare total energy cost across years without volume adjustment
options.b: Benchmark process efficiency and track improvements over time
options.c: Set the facility's utility demand charges for each production line
options.d: Calculate boiler combustion efficiency from units of production

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing raw totals ignores production changes; intensity metrics normalize energy by output.
distractorExplanations.c: Demand charges come from the tariff and metered peak kW; intensity metrics are internal benchmarks.
distractorExplanations.d: Combustion efficiency comes from flue gas O2 and temperature; BTU per unit covers the whole process.

options.a: Capacity, pressure requirements, site access, and lifecycle cost
options.b: Fuel type alone, since package units can burn natural gas only
options.c: Stack height and the local air permit's opacity limit for the site
options.d: Efficiency rating, since field-erected units are rated more efficient

distractorExplanations.b: Package boilers are available for gas, oil, and dual fuel; fuel type alone does not decide package versus field-erected.
distractorExplanations.c: Stack and opacity limits affect emissions design for either type; selection depends mainly on capacity and access.
distractorExplanations.d: Efficiency depends on design and operation, not construction method; field erection is driven by size and pressure.

options.a: Building owners to install onsite renewables sized to a set share of their annual load
options.b: Utilities or suppliers to procure a percentage of energy from renewable sources
options.c: Utilities to offer net metering to customers with renewable systems
options.d: Large facilities to cut energy intensity by a set percentage each year

distractorExplanations.a: RPS obligations fall on load-serving entities, not building owners; onsite mandates are separate building code provisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Net metering is a separate interconnection and billing policy; an RPS sets a renewable share in the supply portfolio.
distractorExplanations.d: Energy intensity reduction targets are efficiency policies such as federal goals, not renewable portfolio standards.

options.a: Replacing traps after a visible plume shows at the vent line
options.b: Replacing every trap on a fixed five-year cycle without testing
options.c: Regular inspection and replacement because failed traps waste fuel
options.d: Installing bypass valves so failed traps can be left open in service

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for visible plumes misses many failed traps; scheduled testing finds failures before major losses accumulate.
distractorExplanations.b: Blanket replacement wastes money on good traps and misses early failures; testing-based programs are better.
distractorExplanations.d: Open bypasses pass live steam continuously; bypasses are for maintenance isolation, not ongoing service.

cem-readiness-check-industrial-boiler-re.explanation: Effective trap management reduces live steam loss, improves safety, and supports boiler efficiency. Failed traps can also damage piping.

options.a: Running base-load equipment only during on-peak periods
options.b: Shifting discretionary loads to off-peak periods
options.c: Raising thermostat setpoints during off-peak hours
options.d: Increasing power factor without changing load schedule

distractorExplanations.a: Operating during on-peak periods increases exposure to the highest energy rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Thermostat changes affect consumption but do not inherently align loads with lower-priced periods.
distractorExplanations.d: Power factor correction affects demand/reactive charges, not TOU energy pricing by itself.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: TOU rates charge different energy prices by time period. Moving flexible loads to off-peak hours lowers the energy ($/kWh) portion of the bill. Off-peak periods are when energy prices are lower.

options.a: Preliminary utility bill analysis and benchmarking against peers
options.b: A list of low-cost and no-cost measures from a walk-through
options.c: Investment-grade modeling with measured data for capital projects
options.d: Detailed energy-use breakdown and savings calculations

distractorExplanations.a: Bill analysis and benchmarking are part of the preliminary energy use analysis before Level I; they are not Level II additions.
distractorExplanations.b: Low-cost/no-cost measures from a walk-through are the Level I deliverable, not the added Level II requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Investment-grade analysis of capital-intensive projects is Level III, which goes beyond the Level II survey and analysis.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Level II expands on Level I with more detailed survey data, end-use breakdowns, quantified savings, and economic evaluation of recommended measures. Level II also includes economic analysis for recommended ECMs.

options.a: Billing demand is set at 80% of each month's own measured peak demand
options.b: The customer pays demand charges on 80% of the yearly average peak
options.c: Demand charges apply only in months when the peak exceeds 80% of contract capacity
options.d: The customer may pay demand charges based on a floor even if actual peak is lower

distractorExplanations.a: The ratchet compares against 80% of the prior 12-month peak; it does not discount the current month's own peak.
distractorExplanations.b: Ratchets use the highest peak in the lookback window, not the average; one spike can set the floor for a year.
distractorExplanations.c: Ratchets set a minimum billing demand from past peaks; they do not limit charges to months above a capacity threshold.

options.a: First-year savings divided by installed cost
options.b: Discounted payback period at the cost of capital
options.c: Savings-to-investment ratio without discounting
options.d: Net present value (NPV) using a discount rate

distractorExplanations.b: Discounted payback adds the time value of money but still ignores cash flows after the payback point.
distractorExplanations.c: An undiscounted savings-to-investment ratio sums cash flows but ignores the time value of money.
distractorExplanations.a: That ratio is a simplified metric, not a full lifecycle evaluation.

options.a: Retrofit savings are isolated with continuous measurement of all key parameters over time
options.b: Whole-facility savings must be determined using utility bill regression
options.c: Individual equipment retrofit savings are isolated with periodic short-term measurements
options.d: Savings are estimated with a calibrated whole-building simulation model

distractorExplanations.a: Measuring all parameters continuously within the retrofit boundary is Option B; Option A measures key parameters and stipulates others.
distractorExplanations.d: Calibrated simulation is Option D, used when baseline or reporting data are missing or interactive effects are complex.
distractorExplanations.b: Whole-facility utility analysis aligns more with Option C or D approaches.

options.a: Mandatory minimum efficiency requirements for building systems and envelope
options.b: Voluntary design guidelines that owners may follow to qualify for rebates
options.c: Above-code efficiency targets used for LEED or green building certification
options.d: Retrofit requirements for all existing buildings immediately

distractorExplanations.b: Adopted codes are enforceable through permits; voluntary guidelines tied to rebates describe utility program criteria.
distractorExplanations.c: Above-code targets belong to rating systems like LEED or stretch codes; the base code sets mandatory minimums.
distractorExplanations.d: Existing building retrofits are typically addressed by separate policies, not new-construction code alone.

options.a: First-year energy savings and the installed cost of the new boiler
options.b: Sunk costs already spent on the existing boiler's original purchase
options.c: Ongoing maintenance, fuel, and replacement costs over the analysis period
options.d: Initial capital cost, including design and installation contractor fees

distractorExplanations.a: Simple payback already uses first-year savings and installed cost; LCC adds the multi-year operating costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Sunk costs are excluded from both LCC and payback because they do not change with the replacement decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Initial capital cost is included in simple payback; LCC is distinguished by adding ongoing and future costs.

options.a: Adjust consumption for weather variation when tracking performance
options.b: Calculate the facility's power factor penalties from monthly kVAR
options.c: Separate base load from end uses so submetering is no longer needed
options.d: Forecast next month's billing demand ratchet from degree-day trends

distractorExplanations.b: Power factor uses kW and kVAR from metering; degree days have no role in reactive power charges.
distractorExplanations.c: Degree-day regression separates weather-dependent from base load but cannot replace end-use submetering detail.
distractorExplanations.d: Ratchets come from tariff rules and recorded peaks; HDD/CDD normalization adjusts consumption for weather.

options.a: An ESPC or performance contract where savings guarantee repayment
options.b: A preliminary bill review to rank buildings in a portfolio for study
options.c: A walk-through to list no-cost and low-cost measures for a small office
options.d: A Level II survey to estimate savings for measures with short paybacks

distractorExplanations.b: Ranking buildings from bills is a preliminary energy use analysis, the step before even a Level I audit.
distractorExplanations.c: Walk-through identification of low-cost measures is a Level I audit, far short of investment-grade rigor.
distractorExplanations.d: Level II suits most ECM decisions; Level III is reserved for capital-intensive projects such as financed ESPCs.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Level III audits provide the rigor, measurement, and risk analysis needed when savings estimates underpin financing guarantees in ESPCs or similar arrangements. The guaranteed savings repay third-party financing.

options.a: Site EUI to the building's own three-year average consumption
options.b: Weather-normalized site EUI to the ASHRAE 90.1 code baseline
options.c: Annual energy cost per square foot to the regional utility average
options.d: Actual source EUI to the national median for similar building types

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing to the building's own history is trend tracking; the 1-100 score compares source EUI to national peers.
distractorExplanations.b: Code-baseline comparisons are used for modeling compliance; Portfolio Manager scores use source EUI versus a national peer group.
distractorExplanations.c: Cost per square foot depends on rates; the ENERGY STAR score uses source energy intensity, not dollars.

options.a: The project creates value on a discounted basis despite a long simple payback
options.b: NPV and payback should agree, so one of the analyses contains an error
options.c: The project should be rejected because payback exceeds 5 years
options.d: Positive NPV means the IRR must be below the 6% discount rate

distractorExplanations.b: NPV and payback measure different things and often diverge for long-lived measures; disagreement is not an error.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed payback cutoff ignores savings after payback; a positive NPV at the 6% rate shows the project adds value.
distractorExplanations.d: Positive NPV at 6% means the IRR is above 6%, not below; IRR is the rate at which NPV equals zero.

options.a: Appliance and equipment efficiency standards set by DOE for manufacturers
options.b: Energy Policy Act tax deductions for efficient commercial buildings (179D)
options.c: ENERGY STAR labeling for buildings that score 75 or higher in Portfolio Manager benchmarking
options.d: Federal energy management requirements such as EISA/ECPA energy intensity goals

distractorExplanations.a: DOE appliance standards apply to products sold nationwide; federal building targets come from EISA/NECPA mandates.
distractorExplanations.b: Section 179D is a tax deduction for efficient buildings; it does not set mandatory federal agency reduction targets.
distractorExplanations.c: ENERGY STAR certification is a voluntary recognition program, not a mandated energy reduction target for agencies.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Federal statutes and executive orders establish energy intensity reduction targets and reporting for federal agencies, driving efficiency in government facilities. These goals require energy intensity reduction.

options.a: Cover the single month just before installation to reflect the latest operating mode
options.b: Represent pre-retrofit conditions with sufficient data to characterize normal operation
options.c: Include the installation period so that construction effects are averaged into it
options.d: Use design-day equipment ratings to represent full-load operation

distractorExplanations.a: One month cannot capture seasonal swings; baselines usually span a full operating cycle, often 12 months.
distractorExplanations.c: The installation period is excluded from both baseline and reporting periods because it is not normal operation.
distractorExplanations.d: Nameplate or design-day ratings do not reflect actual operating patterns; the baseline uses measured pre-retrofit data.

options.a: Pre-cool the building during the high-price event to bank cooling
options.b: Reduce or shift non-critical loads during the high-price event
options.c: Start onsite backup generators once the price event has ended
options.d: Shift critical process loads first while keeping comfort loads on

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-cooling works before the event, at lower prices; doing it during the price spike raises cost and grid stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Backup generation helps the bill only if it runs during the event; starting after the price spike captures no savings.
distractorExplanations.d: Demand response should curtail non-critical loads first; shedding critical process loads risks production and safety.

options.a: The measure has a 90% chance of saving at least 35% of baseline energy
options.b: The estimated savings should be reduced by 35% before any economic analysis is done
options.c: The measure will save exactly 35% with 90% of its cost recovered
options.d: The savings estimate includes quantified uncertainty bounds from the analysis

distractorExplanations.a: The figure is a plus/minus band on the savings estimate, not a 35% share of baseline energy saved with 90% probability.
distractorExplanations.b: Uncertainty describes a range around the estimate; it does not mean savings should be cut by 35% before analysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Uncertainty bands mean savings are not fixed at a single value; 90% is a statistical confidence level, not cost recovery.

options.a: One year of interval demand data with no field survey of installed equipment
options.b: Design drawings and equipment schedules from the original construction set
options.c: Nameplate ratings of major equipment multiplied by 8,760 hours
options.d: 12 months of utility bills plus end-use estimates from survey and spot measurements

distractorExplanations.a: Interval data shows load shape but cannot allocate energy to end uses without an equipment survey.
distractorExplanations.b: Original design documents may not reflect current equipment or operation; balances need actual bills and field data.
distractorExplanations.c: Nameplate times 8,760 overstates use by ignoring load factor and schedules; balances reconcile with actual bills.

options.a: Taxable income in year one that is excluded from the project cash flows
options.b: A reduction in annual energy cost spread evenly over the measure's useful life
options.c: An addition to salvage value at the end of the analysis period
options.d: A reduction in initial capital cost (or equivalent incentive cash flow)

distractorExplanations.a: Rebates belong in the cash flow analysis; excluding them overstates net cost and understates project viability.
distractorExplanations.b: A rebate is a one-time incentive at installation, not a recurring energy cost saving across the measure's life.
distractorExplanations.c: Salvage value is residual worth at the end of the period; rebates arrive at the start and offset capital cost.

options.a: Lighting power density in the open office areas
options.b: Plug load and office equipment energy consumption
options.c: HVAC fan energy serving the office floors
options.d: Peak cooling demand from chillers serving data rooms

distractorExplanations.a: Lighting power is governed by fixture and control choices; ENERGY STAR office equipment targets plug loads.
distractorExplanations.c: Fan energy depends on air handlers and VAV control; ENERGY STAR office equipment affects plug loads directly.
distractorExplanations.d: Chiller demand is an HVAC plant issue; the procurement policy reduces equipment plug loads, with minor cooling side effects.

options.a: Adjust the baseline for production or other relevant independent variables
options.b: Report the 10% drop as savings because production rose at the same time
options.c: Normalize consumption for heating and cooling degree days only
options.d: Reset the baseline to the first post-retrofit year of production

distractorExplanations.b: Unadjusted comparisons mix production effects with the retrofit; savings must be calculated against an adjusted baseline.
distractorExplanations.c: Weather is one variable, but here production changed 20%; the baseline must be adjusted for production too.
distractorExplanations.d: A post-retrofit period cannot serve as the baseline; the pre-retrofit baseline is kept and adjusted.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: M&V protocols require routine adjustments for variables like production, occupancy, or weather so reported savings reflect the ECM, not unrelated activity changes. These adjustments belong in the M&V plan.

options.a: Tenant data access for ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager benchmarking
options.b: Split incentive barriers between landlord and tenant
options.c: Demand charge allocation among multiple tenants
options.d: Free-rider effects in utility rebate programs

distractorExplanations.a: Data access clauses support benchmarking; cost-recovery clauses mainly fix who pays versus who benefits.
distractorExplanations.c: Allocating demand among tenants is a submetering and billing issue; green leases mainly resolve split incentives.
distractorExplanations.d: Free-ridership is a program evaluation concept for rebates; split incentives concern landlord-tenant cost and benefit.

options.a: Spot-indexed volumes expose the buyer to price volatility on those blocks
options.b: Fixed blocks expose the buyer to daily spot price volatility
options.c: Take-or-pay terms require paying for blocks at the daily index price
options.d: Index volumes are capped at the block price, so the risk falls on the supplier

distractorExplanations.b: Block volumes are priced at a fixed contract rate; the volatility risk sits on the index-priced portion.
distractorExplanations.c: Take-or-pay obliges payment for unused contracted volume; it does not reprice fixed blocks at the index.
distractorExplanations.d: No cap is implied; without a collar or cap, index-priced volumes carry the market risk for the buyer.

options.a: Marginal energy rate for the next kWh in the tariff block
options.b: Load factor, average demand divided by peak demand
options.c: Energy use intensity in kBtu per square foot per year
options.d: Average blended energy rate ($/kWh or $/therm equivalent)

distractorExplanations.a: The marginal rate is the cost of the next unit at the current tier or period, not total cost divided by total use.
distractorExplanations.b: Load factor is average kW divided by peak kW over a period, a usage shape metric, not a cost per unit.
distractorExplanations.c: EUI divides energy by floor area, not cost by energy; it measures intensity rather than average unit price.

options.a: Third-party certification of a fixed percent energy reduction
options.b: An environmental management system covering emissions and waste
options.c: A building energy code compliance path for new construction
options.d: A structured energy management system with continual improvement

distractorExplanations.a: ISO 50001 requires demonstrated improvement in energy performance but sets no fixed percentage reduction.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes ISO 14001; ISO 50001 is the energy management system standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Codes such as ASHRAE 90.1 govern design; ISO 50001 is a voluntary organizational management standard.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: ISO 50001 establishes a management system framework—policy, energy review, objectives, monitoring, and corrective action—for continual energy performance improvement. Its elements include policy, planning, and monitoring.

options.a: The initial capital cost and annual savings used to compute it
options.b: Savings occurring after year 4 and the time value of money
options.c: Savings in years 1 through 4 and the project's installed cost
options.d: Energy price escalation during the first year of operation

distractorExplanations.a: Payback is computed from initial cost and annual savings, so it does not ignore them.
