distractorExplanations.c: Payback counts the first four years of savings against installed cost; it ignores savings after recovery.
distractorExplanations.d: First-year escalation is minor; the key omission is all savings beyond year 4 and discounting.

options.a: Detailed end-use breakdowns and savings for each capital measure
options.b: Obvious operational waste and low-cost/no-cost opportunities
options.c: Investment-grade uncertainty analysis for every recommended measure
options.d: Sub-hourly interval data regression for each major end use

distractorExplanations.a: End-use breakdowns and measure-by-measure savings are Level II deliverables, beyond a Level I walk-through.
distractorExplanations.c: Detailed uncertainty and risk analysis is characteristic of Level III investment-grade audits.
distractorExplanations.d: Sub-hourly regression exceeds Level I scope and budget; Level I relies on bills and a brief survey.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Level I focuses on rapid identification of evident waste and no-cost/low-cost measures with preliminary savings direction, not detailed investment-grade analysis. Comfort complaints are also worth recording.

options.a: Reducing on-peak demand and associated demand charges
options.b: Reducing total cooling energy by improving chiller efficiency
options.c: Lowering energy charges by running the chiller during peak hours
options.d: Reducing the facility's off-peak demand ratchet in winter

distractorExplanations.b: Storage shifts when cooling is made; total energy often rises slightly due to storage losses and colder charging.
distractorExplanations.c: Running chillers on-peak is what storage avoids; charging off-peak lowers on-peak kW and demand charges.
distractorExplanations.d: Thermal storage raises off-peak load to cut on-peak demand; it targets summer on-peak charges.

options.a: Financing efficiency upgrades repaid through the monthly utility bill
options.b: Tax credits for efficiency upgrades claimed on state income tax returns
options.c: Financing efficiency upgrades repaid via a special property tax assessment
options.d: Utility rebates for upgrades paid as a credit on the property tax bill

distractorExplanations.a: Repayment on the utility bill is on-bill financing; PACE repays through the property tax assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: State income tax credits are incentives, not financing; PACE is financing repaid via the property tax bill.
distractorExplanations.d: Rebates are grants with no repayment; PACE financing must be repaid over time through the assessment.

options.a: Cooling degree-day normalization of the baseline and reporting period gas use
options.b: Heating degree-day normalization of baseline and reporting period consumption
options.c: Production-based normalization of baseline and reporting period gas consumption
options.d: Comparing reporting period gas use directly with the baseline

distractorExplanations.a: Winter gas use is driven by heating degree days; cooling degree days do not explain space-heating consumption.
distractorExplanations.c: Production adjustment applies when output changes; a warmer winter calls for HDD normalization.
distractorExplanations.d: A direct comparison credits mild-weather reductions to the retrofit, overstating savings.

options.a: Present value of benefits is 1.4 times present value of costs
options.b: Undiscounted savings exceed project cost by 1.4 percent overall
options.c: Simple payback is 1.4 years on the installed project cost
options.d: The internal rate of return on the measure is 40 percent

distractorExplanations.b: BCR is a ratio of present values, not a percent margin; 1.4 means benefits are 140% of costs.
distractorExplanations.c: Payback is years to recover cost; BCR is a dimensionless ratio of discounted benefits to discounted costs.
distractorExplanations.d: IRR is the discount rate yielding zero NPV; a BCR of 1.4 does not translate directly to a 40% return.

options.a: Set mandatory energy reduction targets for each covered building
options.b: Require owners to implement every measure the audit identifies
options.c: Identify efficiency opportunities and inform owners about performance
options.d: Replace annual benchmarking with a one-time audit at sale

distractorExplanations.a: Building performance standards set reduction targets; audit ordinances require assessments, not targets.
distractorExplanations.b: Most audit ordinances require the assessment but leave measure implementation to owner decisions.
distractorExplanations.d: Audit ordinances usually complement benchmarking; time-of-sale disclosure is a different policy design.

options.a: The ECM affects only fixed monthly customer charges
options.b: The project changes consumption at the margin
options.c: The tariff is a flat rate with no tiers or demand
options.d: The utility bill shows a low blended average rate

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed customer charges do not change with consumption; marginal analysis applies to energy and demand avoided.
distractorExplanations.c: Under a pure flat rate, marginal and average costs are equal, so the distinction does not matter there.
distractorExplanations.d: A low average rate says nothing about the next unit's cost; marginal pricing matters when tiers or TOU differ.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Savings should reflect the cost of the next unit of energy avoided—accounting for rate tiers, TOU periods, and demand impacts—not always a simple average rate. Example: kWh avoided at the current rate tier or TOU period.

options.a: Project approval speed by using simple payback as the sole screening test
options.b: Capital budget control by selecting the lowest first-cost bid for each project
options.c: Decision quality by comparing long-term costs rather than first cost alone
options.d: Code compliance by documenting minimum efficiency equipment

distractorExplanations.a: Simple payback is what LCC policies supplement; it ignores savings beyond payback and discounting.
distractorExplanations.b: Lowest first cost is the approach LCC replaces; LCC weighs energy, maintenance, and replacements.
distractorExplanations.d: Code compliance sets minimum efficiency; LCC policy guides choices among options above that floor.

options.a: The M&V plan including measurement boundary and reporting period
options.b: The savings report issued after each reporting period
options.c: The baseline model regression equation and its coefficients
options.d: The ECM installation contract's scope of work section

distractorExplanations.b: Savings reports present results after the fact; the M&V plan defines the claim and boundary beforehand.
distractorExplanations.c: The baseline model is one component; the M&V plan sets the boundary, option, and reporting period.
distractorExplanations.d: The construction scope defines what is installed, not how savings are measured or bounded.

options.a: Estimating consumption from a calibrated model when meter data are missing
options.b: Temporarily logging a single end use for a few weeks with portable meters
options.c: Independent verification metering installed alongside the utility meter
options.d: Using the utility meter's pulse output to feed the campus BAS

distractorExplanations.a: Filling gaps with a calibrated model is an Option D or data-estimation method, not shadow metering.
distractorExplanations.b: Short-term portable logging is spot or short-term metering for Option A, not permanent parallel metering.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse output sharing reuses the utility meter's data; a shadow meter is a separate, independent meter.

options.a: $11,600 including energy and summer demand reduction
options.b: $1,600 from summer demand reduction alone
options.c: $10,000 from energy savings alone at $0.10
options.d: $14,800 including energy and 12 months of demand

distractorExplanations.b: $1,600 is the demand piece only (50 x $8 x 4); it omits the $10,000 of energy savings.
distractorExplanations.c: This counts 100,000 x $0.10 = $10,000 and omits the $1,600 summer demand savings.
distractorExplanations.d: Applying demand savings for 12 months (50 x $8 x 12 = $4,800) ignores that peak reduction lasts 4 summer months.

options.a: IRR exceeds 10% or NPV is positive at a 10% discount rate
options.b: IRR exceeds 10% and simple payback is under the 10-year mark
options.c: NPV is positive at the company's 6% cost of borrowing
options.d: Simple ROI exceeds 10% in the first year of operation

distractorExplanations.b: Adding a payback cutoff is not part of the hurdle test; the rate test is IRR above 10% or NPV above zero at 10%.
distractorExplanations.c: Testing at 6% instead of the 10% hurdle rate approves projects that fail the corporate threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: First-year ROI ignores the time value of money and later cash flows; hurdle rates apply to IRR or NPV.

options.a: Prescriptive compliance with each envelope and HVAC minimum
options.b: Performance-based or total building energy compliance modeling
options.c: Envelope trade-off compliance using COMcheck envelope UA
options.d: Mandatory provisions compliance applied to every project

distractorExplanations.a: The prescriptive path requires each component to meet its minimum and allows no cross-system trade-offs.
distractorExplanations.c: Envelope UA trade-offs allow swaps within the envelope, not between envelope and HVAC efficiency.
distractorExplanations.d: Mandatory provisions apply under every path and cannot be traded off; they are not a trade-off path.

options.a: Measuring leak flow in cfm directly with ultrasonic detectors
options.b: Estimating compressor full-load kW from motor nameplate data
options.c: Translating technical waste into dollar terms to prioritize repairs
options.d: Setting the leak repair budget from last year's maintenance spend

distractorExplanations.a: Ultrasonic detection locates leaks; COWE converts the resulting waste into dollars for decisions.
distractorExplanations.b: Nameplate kW is an input; COWE translates wasted energy into an annual cost for prioritizing repairs.
distractorExplanations.d: Historical spend ignores the size of the waste; COWE ties priorities to the dollar value of losses.

options.a: Lets utilities earn a return on efficiency spending like capital assets
options.b: Separates generation from distribution ownership to allow competition
options.c: Reduces utility disincentive to sell less energy when efficiency reduces sales
options.d: Lowers customer rates whenever efficiency programs reduce utility sales

distractorExplanations.a: Earning a return on program spending is a performance incentive or capitalization; decoupling breaks the revenue-sales link.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes restructuring or unbundling; decoupling adjusts revenue recovery independent of sales volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Decoupling true-ups can raise per-unit rates slightly when sales fall; it protects revenue rather than lowering rates.

options.a: Decrease the present value of savings because prices are discounted
options.b: Increase the nominal value of future savings compared with flat prices
options.c: Cancel out the discount rate so that real and nominal values match
options.d: Increase first-year savings by 3% compared with flat prices

distractorExplanations.a: Escalation raises future savings; discounting is applied separately and does not reverse the escalation effect.
distractorExplanations.c: Escalation and discounting are separate; they offset only if the rates are equal, and discounting still applies.
distractorExplanations.d: Escalation starts after the base year; first-year savings are at current prices, and later years grow.

options.a: A major unrelated change occurs, such as adding a new production line
options.b: Production volume rises 15% within its normal range in the M&V plan
options.c: Weather is warmer than normal but within the regression's data range
options.d: The ECM's savings fall short of the audit estimate by about 20%

distractorExplanations.b: Production within the planned range is a routine adjustment variable already in the baseline model.
distractorExplanations.c: Weather variation within the model's range is handled by routine adjustments, not non-routine ones.
distractorExplanations.d: A savings shortfall is a performance finding, not a change in static factors requiring non-routine adjustment.

cem-readiness-check-policy-audits-econom.explanation: Non-routine adjustments address unforeseen changes outside the M&V plan's routine variables, such as significant capacity additions or shutdowns. The change occurs mid-period.

options.a: A measure's simple payback and its first-year energy savings
options.b: A measure's capital cost and its share of the total project budget
options.c: A measure's cost per unit of energy saved and potential savings volume
options.d: A measure's emissions per kWh saved and the grid's marginal emissions rate

distractorExplanations.a: MACC bar height is cost per unit abated and width is volume; payback is not the plotted metric.
distractorExplanations.b: Capital cost alone ignores savings; MACC bars show cost-effectiveness per unit saved and volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Emission factors convert energy to carbon but are not the bars; MACC bars plot cost per unit and potential.

options.a: Determining exact end-use energy shares without a site survey
options.b: Identifying load shapes, peak drivers, and operational anomalies
options.c: Verifying the utility's revenue meter accuracy for billing disputes
options.d: Calculating monthly power factor penalties from kWh data

distractorExplanations.a: Interval data shows when loads occur but not which equipment; a site survey still links shapes to end uses.
distractorExplanations.c: Accuracy disputes need meter testing; interval data reveals load shape and peak timing.
distractorExplanations.d: Power factor needs kVAR or kVA data; kW/kWh interval data alone cannot compute it.

options.a: Raise the hot deck setpoint to recover warm-up faster.
options.b: Add zone reheat coils to correct the cold deck overcooling.
options.c: Reset and sequence deck setpoints to eliminate overlap.
options.d: Lower the cold deck setpoint to improve zone dehumidification.

distractorExplanations.a: A higher hot deck temperature increases mixing losses with the cold deck; the setpoint overlap remains.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding reheat increases simultaneous heating and cooling; the deck sequencing must be fixed first.
distractorExplanations.d: A colder cold deck widens the gap the hot deck must offset, increasing simultaneous heating and cooling waste.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: Overlapping heating and cooling setpoints waste energy through concurrent conditioning. Correcting sequencing and setpoints is the highest-leverage first fix before adding capacity. Correct sequencing also enables economizer-friendly operation.

options.a: Thermal bridging and air leakage paths that increase heating load.
options.b: Moisture-saturated insulation from roof leaks inside wall cavities.
options.c: Effective insulation that keeps heat inside along the studs and frames.
options.d: Solar gain reflected off adjacent glazing during the early morning.

distractorExplanations.b: Wet insulation shows as irregular patches, not regular lines at every stud and window perimeter.
distractorExplanations.c: Warm exterior streaks mean heat escaping; effective insulation would show uniformly cool exterior surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflections shift with viewing angle and sun position; stud-line patterns on a cold morning indicate conduction.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: IR patterns highlighting framing and openings typically reveal conduction bridges and infiltration, which raise heating energy and create cold spots. They also cause local discomfort.

options.a: Mixed-air temperature tracks outdoor-air temperature closely.
options.b: Return-air temperature tracks the zone setpoint closely.
options.c: Supply-air temperature tracks the discharge setpoint closely.
options.d: Return-air CO2 rises steadily while dampers are at minimum.

distractorExplanations.b: Return air near setpoint indicates satisfied zones; it says nothing about outdoor-air damper position.
distractorExplanations.c: Supply air on setpoint shows the heating coil is keeping up, not that excess outdoor air is entering.
distractorExplanations.d: Rising CO2 suggests under-ventilation, the opposite of a stuck-open outdoor-air damper.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: If mixed air follows outdoor air in cold weather and heating is maxed, excess outdoor air is likely entering through a damper that is open or leaking. Heating valves staying near full open confirm the diagnosis.

options.a: Air-sealing and weatherstripping to reduce uncontrolled infiltration.
options.b: Replacing single glazing with low-e triple glazing on all facades.
options.c: Adding interior insulation behind spandrel panels before sealing.
options.d: Applying reflective window film to reduce winter heat loss.

distractorExplanations.b: Reglazing is costly and its heating savings vary; infiltration in leaky curtain walls usually dominates first.
distractorExplanations.c: Insulating before sealing leaves air bypassing the insulation, so the savings are less reliable.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflective films mainly cut solar gain and can raise heating load; they do little for infiltration.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-04.explanation: Infiltration often dominates heating loss in leaky curtain-wall buildings; sealing is cost-effective and improves comfort before capital HVAC upgrades. Sealing comes before adding insulation or HVAC capacity.

options.a: Whether the setback temperature stays above the space dew point to avoid condensation.
options.b: Whether radiation and air-side recovery sequences can restore comfort by occupancy.
options.c: Whether VAV box minimum airflows meet ventilation rates during unoccupied hours.
options.d: Whether chilled-water reset limits allow economizer operation during setback.

distractorExplanations.a: Condensation risk applies to cooling setup in humid climates; winter setback with radiation is a morning recovery issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventilation minimums apply during occupancy; unoccupied setback mode can close outdoor air.
distractorExplanations.d: Chilled-water reset is a cooling plant strategy; night setback evaluation centers on morning heating recovery.

cem-readiness-check-hvac-envelope-bas-05.explanation: Aggressive setback without adequate morning warmup capacity or sequencing can cause recovery peaks, complaints, and demand charges. Recovery must also avoid excessive morning peak demand.
